query.original_query: how LLMs organize relational knowledge, shared subspaces across relations, knowledge graph structure in representations

sub_queries.semantic_query: organization of relational knowledge in LLMs, shared subspaces across relations, knowledge graph structure encoded in intermediate representations, probing and causal discovery of relational facts
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how relational knowledge is organized within the intermediate representations of large language models, focusing on whether shared subspaces encode structural properties of knowledge graphs. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we analyze the internal representations of factual triples across multiple relation types. Our analysis reveals that relational facts sharing similar semantic roles or relation types cluster in low-dimensional subspaces of the residual stream, consistent with the hypothesis that models learn a compressed relational geometry. We find that these shared subspaces are partially localized to specific MLP layers and attention heads, and that intervening on these subspaces can alter model predictions for multiple related facts simultaneously. Probing experiments show that linear classifiers can decode relation type from these subspaces with high accuracy, and causal mediation analysis confirms that these representations are causally implicated in factual recall. Results suggest that LLMs encode a structured, graph-like organization of relational knowledge within their hidden states, rather than storing facts as isolated entries.

sub_queries.semantic_query: how LLMs organize relational knowledge, shared subspaces across relations, knowledge graph structure in representations
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated how large language models organize relational knowledge by examining shared representational subspaces across distinct relation types. Using probing classifiers and representational similarity analysis on hidden states from multiple transformer-based models, we tested whether relations such as "is-a," "part-of," and "caused-by" occupy geometrically aligned subspaces within the same layer. Stimuli consisted of triples from curated knowledge graph subsets, with controlled entity frequency and relation ambiguity. Results indicate that models encode relational structure in partially overlapping subspaces, with higher alignment for semantically similar relations. Representational geometry showed systematic clustering by relation type, and the degree of subspace overlap correlated with the relational distance in external knowledge graphs. Control analyses ruled out simple lexical or positional confounds. These findings support the hypothesis that LLMs develop an internal organization of relational knowledge that mirrors graph-theoretic structure, with shared subspaces reflecting common relational semantics rather than surface form.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Probing Relational Knowledge in Language Models via Word Analogies
papers.research_question: Do transformer-based language models hold sufficient relational information to classify an analogy as being true or false, and how do they perform on three specific aspects: directionality, type distinctions, and the relation itself?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a word analogy-based probing methodology to assess relational knowledge in PLMs, finding that PLMs excel at capturing directionality and type distinctions but struggle with fine-grained relational distinctions.
papers.conclusion: PLMs are accurate at capturing directionality and word categories in relations, but struggle with fine-grained relational distinctions, as shown by the challenging random probe.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs are extremely accurate at capturing directionality of relations and distinguishing types, but have room for improvement in fine-grained relational distinctions (random probe).
Larger models (RoBERTa-large) consistently outperform smaller ones (RoBERTa-base) in probing relational knowledge.
In unsupervised settings, PLMs perform better on fine-grained distinctions compared to static embeddings, indicating that contextual information helps.
Word frequency does not significantly affect performance for most relation types, except for a few (e.g., male-female and adj:comparative).
Performance varies by relation type, with one/many-to-many and bidirectional relations showing expected patterns (poor performance on random probe for one/many-to-many and on reverse probe for bidirectional).
papers.limitation:
Only English language is analyzed, limiting conclusions for other languages.
Limited number of models and configurations/prompts explored.
Word analogies may be prone to external biases or confounding factors.
Data limited to BATS dataset (40 relations, biased towards certain categories).
papers.abstract: Understanding relational knowledge plays an integral part in natural language comprehension. When it comes to pre-trained language models (PLM), prior work has been focusing on probing relational knowledge this by filling the blanks in pre-defined prompts such as “The capital of France is —". However, these probes may be affected by the co-occurrence of target relation words and entities (e.g. “capital”, “France” and “Paris”) in the pre-training corpus. In this work, we extend these probing methodologies leveraging analogical proportions as a proxy to probe relational knowledge in transformer-based PLMs without directly presenting the desired relation. In particular, we analysed the ability of PLMs to understand (1) the directionality of a given relation (e.g. Paris-France is not the same as France-Paris); (2) the ability to distinguish types on a given relation (both France and Japan are countries); and (3) the relation itself (Paris is the capital of France, but not Rome). Our results show how PLMs are extremely accurate at (1) and (2), but have clear room for improvement for (3). To better understand the reasons behind this behaviour and mistakes made by PLMs, we provide an extended quantitative analysis based on relevant factors such as frequency.

papers.title: Does Knowledge Localization Hold True? Surprising Differences Between Entity and Relation Perspectives in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether entity and relational knowledge are stored equivalently in language models and where relational knowledge is localized within model parameters.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that entity and relational knowledge are stored separately in language models, with relational knowledge encoded in both MLP and attention layers, challenging previous assumptions that knowledge is primarily localized in MLP weights.
papers.conclusion: This paper reveals that relational knowledge in LLMs is encoded not only in MLP layers but also significantly in attention modules, highlighting the complexity of knowledge storage mechanisms and providing a new foundation for future research in model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Editing entity knowledge does not equivalently edit relational knowledge, and vice versa, indicating they are not interchangeable.
Relational knowledge is localized in both MLP and attention layers, unlike entity knowledge which prior work suggested is primarily in MLP layers.
Knowledge storage location identified through causal tracing differs significantly between entity and relation perspectives.
Model editing from entity and relation perspectives yields inconsistent outcomes, questioning the validity of previous knowledge localization methods.
Factual knowledge is not stored as a single unit; relations and entities are represented separately within model parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models encapsulate knowledge and have demonstrated superior performance on various natural language processing tasks. Recent studies have localized this knowledge to specific model parameters, such as the MLP weights in intermediate layers. This study investigates the differences between entity and relational knowledge through knowledge editing. Our findings reveal that entity and relational knowledge cannot be directly transferred or mapped to each other. This result is unexpected, as logically, modifying the entity or the relation within the same knowledge triplet should yield equivalent outcomes. To further elucidate the differences between entity and relational knowledge, we employ causal analysis to investigate how relational knowledge is stored in pre-trained models. Contrary to prior research suggesting that knowledge is stored in MLP weights, our experiments demonstrate that relational knowledge is also significantly encoded in attention modules. This insight highlights the multifaceted nature of knowledge storage in language models, underscoring the complexity of manipulating specific types of knowledge within these models.

papers.title: Relational Knowledge Distillation Using Fine-tuned Function Vectors
papers.research_question: How can relational knowledge be distilled from LLMs and refined to improve performance on relation-based tasks and analogical reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning function vectors derived from causal mediation analysis with few examples improves relational task performance and human alignment; these vectors can be linearly combined into composite function vectors to solve challenging analogy problems.
papers.conclusion: Relational knowledge can be distilled from LLMs through function vectors, and fine-tuning and composing these vectors enables human-like analogical reasoning, advancing model interpretability and reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuned function vectors (FFVs) outperform initial function vectors on zero-shot relation tasks across model sizes.
FFVs show stronger alignment with human similarity judgments of semantic relations compared to initial vectors.
Composite function vectors (CFVs) significantly improve performance on challenging far-analogy problems, especially cross-domain analogies.
The improvements from FFVs and CFVs are consistent across both small and large language models.
Effective learning is achieved with very small training sets (e.g., as few as 10-20 word pairs per relation).
papers.limitation:
The study's analogies are restricted to four-term problems (A:B::C:D), while analogical reasoning extends to more complex structures like narratives and stories.
The hierarchical nature of human relational representations (e.g., subtypes of whole-part relations) is not fully addressed; it is unclear if LLMs naturally acquire such hierarchies.
future_direction: Expand the framework to analogies between narratives and stories, which involve more complex relational structures.
Investigate whether LLMs naturally acquire hierarchical structures in their relational representations or require additional alignment.
papers.abstract: Representing relations between concepts is a core prerequisite for intelligent systems to make sense of the world. Recent work using causal mediation analysis has shown that a small set of attention heads encodes task representation in in-context learning, captured in a compact representation known as the function vector. We show that fine-tuning function vectors with only a small set of examples (about 20 word pairs) yields better performance on relation-based word-completion tasks than using the original vectors derived from causal mediation analysis. These improvements hold for both small and large language models. Moreover, the fine-tuned function vectors yield improved decoding performance for relation words and show stronger alignment with human similarity judgments of semantic relations. Next, we introduce the composite function vector - a weighted combination of fine-tuned function vectors - to extract relational knowledge and support analogical reasoning. At inference time, inserting this composite vector into LLM activations markedly enhances performance on challenging analogy problems drawn from cognitive science and SAT benchmarks. Our results highlight the potential of activation patching as a controllable mechanism for encoding and manipulating relational knowledge, advancing both the interpretability and reasoning capabilities of large language models.

papers.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What does 'linear representation' actually mean in the context of language models, and how can we make sense of geometric notions like cosine similarity and projection in the representation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the linear representation hypothesis using counterfactuals, connects it to linear probing and model steering, and introduces a causal inner product that unifies different notions of linear representation and respects semantic structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper formalizes linear representation and shows that all natural variants of this notion can be unified through a causal inner product, which plays a critical role in enabling interpretation and control of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Concepts are represented as directions in the unembedding space, supporting the linear representation hypothesis.
The proposed causal inner product respects causal separability, making causally separable concepts approximately orthogonal.
The unembedding representation of a concept can be used as a linear probe to predict the concept from context embeddings.
The embedding representation (obtained via the causal inner product) can be used for intervention, steering the model's output towards a target concept.
The Euclidean inner product does not always capture semantic structure, while the causal inner product does.
papers.abstract: Informally, the 'linear representation hypothesis' is the idea that high-level concepts are represented linearly as directions in some representation space. In this paper, we address two closely related questions: What does "linear representation" actually mean? And, how do we make sense of geometric notions (e.g., cosine similarity or projection) in the representation space? To answer these, we use the language of counterfactuals to give two formalizations of "linear representation", one in the output (word) representation space, and one in the input (sentence) space. We then prove these connect to linear probing and model steering, respectively. To make sense of geometric notions, we use the formalization to identify a particular (non-Euclidean) inner product that respects language structure in a sense we make precise. Using this causal inner product, we show how to unify all notions of linear representation. In particular, this allows the construction of probes and steering vectors using counterfactual pairs. Experiments with LLaMA-2 demonstrate the existence of linear representations of concepts, the connection to interpretation and control, and the fundamental role of the choice of inner product.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: BERTnesia: Investigating the capture and forgetting of knowledge in BERT
papers.research_question: How is relational knowledge distributed across BERT's layers, and how does fine-tuning affect the retention and forgetting of such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a layerwise probing framework for BERT and finds that intermediate layers contain significant relational knowledge, which is forgotten during fine-tuning, with the extent of forgetting depending on the fine-tuning objective.
papers.conclusion: The proposed layerwise probing framework reveals that BERT stores significant knowledge in intermediate layers, which is forgotten during fine-tuning, with ranking tasks mitigating forgetting more than QA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers contain a substantial amount of knowledge (17-60% of total knowledge) that is not present in the last layer.
Relational knowledge emerges at varying rates across layers, with some relation types doubling in the last layer and others being maximally captured in intermediate layers.
Fine-tuning causes forgetting of relational knowledge, but the amount of forgetting is influenced by the fine-tuning objective, not the dataset size.
Ranking models forget the least and retain more knowledge in their final layer compared to QA models.
The total knowledge in BERT is underestimated when only the last layer is probed.
papers.limitation:
Probing with cloze statements may conflate task-specific knowledge (masked word prediction) with factual knowledge, especially for MLM models.
Probes are limited to single-token factual knowledge, excluding multi-word entities and relations.
future_direction: Investigating ranking models with different training objectives (pointwise, pairwise, listwise).
Studying knowledge-intensive QA models like answer generation models.
Applying the framework to study variants of BERT architecture and pre-training methods.
papers.abstract: Probing complex language models has recently revealed several insights into linguistic and semantic patterns found in the learned representations. In this paper, we probe BERT specifically to understand and measure the relational knowledge it captures. We utilize knowledge base completion tasks to probe every layer of pre-trained as well as fine-tuned BERT (ranking, question answering, NER). Our findings show that knowledge is not just contained in BERT's final layers. Intermediate layers contribute a significant amount (17-60%) to the total knowledge found. Probing intermediate layers also reveals how different types of knowledge emerge at varying rates. When BERT is fine-tuned, relational knowledge is forgotten but the extent of forgetting is impacted by the fine-tuning objective but not the size of the dataset. We found that ranking models forget the least and retain more knowledge in their final layer. We release our code on github 1 to repeat the experiments.

papers.title: Linearity of Relation Decoding in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformer language models represent and decode relational knowledge? Is the decoding process for relations linear?
papers.core_contribution: For a subset of relations, transformer language models decode relational knowledge via a linear transformation on the subject representation, which can be estimated from the model's Jacobian.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models employ linear relational embeddings for a subset of relations, revealing a simple, interpretable, but heterogeneously deployed knowledge representation strategy.
papers.key_findings:
For 48% of the relations tested, the relation decoding is well-approximated by a linear relational embedding (LRE).
LREs can be estimated from the model's Jacobian using a few examples and are causally involved in the model's predictions.
Some relations are not linearly decodable, indicating that LMs use heterogeneous knowledge representation strategies.
The attribute lens, built from LREs, visualizes relational knowledge in intermediate layers and can reveal latent knowledge.
LREs can be used to edit subject representations to control model output, demonstrating causal influence.
papers.limitation:
The dataset only includes 47 relations, limiting the generality of the findings.
Evaluation uses first-token correctness, which may lead to false positives when multiple objects share the same first token.
The dataset assumes a single correct object per subject, but some relations may have multiple correct answers.
future_direction: Extending the method to multi-token objects and relations with multiple correct answers.
Applying LREs to mitigate biases in models.
papers.abstract: Much of the knowledge encoded in transformer language models (LMs) may be expressed in terms of relations: relations between words and their synonyms, entities and their attributes, etc. We show that, for a subset of relations, this computation is well-approximated by a single linear transformation on the subject representation. Linear relation representations may be obtained by constructing a first-order approximation to the LM from a single prompt, and they exist for a variety of factual, commonsense, and linguistic relations. However, we also identify many cases in which LM predictions capture relational knowledge accurately, but this knowledge is not linearly encoded in their representations. Our results thus reveal a simple, interpretable, but heterogeneously deployed knowledge representation strategy in transformer LMs.

papers.title: Unveiling LLMs: The Evolution of Latent Representations in a Dynamic Knowledge Graph
papers.research_question: Which factual knowledge do LLMs use to assess input truthfulness? How does this knowledge evolve across layers? Are there any distinctive patterns in its evolution?
papers.core_contribution: An end-to-end framework that decodes factual knowledge from LLM latent representations (as ground predicates) and represents its layer-wise evolution as a dynamic knowledge graph, enabling local and global interpretability analyses.
papers.conclusion: By decoding semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this framework advances our understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process and the mechanistic interpretability of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Entity centrality is highlighted in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluations.
The global analysis reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts.
Early layers focus on syntax and entity resolution, while middle layers are crucial for factual knowledge resolution.
The framework can identify representation errors, such as entity confusion, duplication, and example leakage, that lead to incorrect evaluations.
The model's classification performance shows an imbalance, with higher precision for true claims and higher recall for false claims on FEVER, and more balanced recall on CLIMATE-FEVER.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive capacity to recall a vast range of factual knowledge. However, understanding their underlying reasoning and internal mechanisms in exploiting this knowledge remains a key research area. This work unveils the factual information an LLM represents internally for sentence-level claim verification. We propose an end-to-end framework to decode factual knowledge embedded in token representations from a vector space to a set of ground predicates, showing its layer-wise evolution using a dynamic knowledge graph. Our framework employs activation patching, a vector-level technique that alters a token representation during inference, to extract encoded knowledge. Accordingly, we neither rely on training nor external models. Using factual and common-sense claims from two claim verification datasets, we showcase interpretability analyses at local and global levels. The local analysis highlights entity centrality in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluation. On the other hand, the global reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts. By interpreting semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this work enhances the understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge, such as materials property prediction.
Informing the design of downstream embedding-based tasks.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs) represent and recall multi-associated attributes across transformer layers. We show that intermediate layers encode factual knowledge by superimposing related attributes in overlapping spaces, along with effective recall even when attributes are not explicitly prompted. In contrast, later layers refine linguistic patterns and progressively separate attribute representations, optimizing task-specific outputs while appropriately narrowing attribute recall. We identify diverse encoding patterns including, for the first time, the observation of 3D spiral structures when exploring information related to the periodic table of elements. Our findings reveal a dynamic transition in attribute representations across layers, contributing to mechanistic interpretability and providing insights for understanding how LLMs handle complex, interrelated knowledge.

papers.title: Dissecting Recall of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Language Models
papers.research_question: How do auto-regressive language models internally retrieve factual associations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-step internal mechanism for factual attribute extraction in auto-regressive LMs, involving subject enrichment by early MLPs, relation propagation, and attribute extraction by attention heads.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations are stored in lower layers and extracted by MLP sublayers to form attribute-rich subject representations; upon a query, the attribute is extracted by MHSA sublayers whose parameters often encode subject-attribute mappings.
papers.key_findings:
Critical information flows from relation and then subject positions to the prediction via specific attention edges.
Subject representations are enriched with multiple attributes by early MLP sublayers.
Attribute extraction is primarily performed by upper MHSA sublayers via attention heads that encode subject-attribute mappings.
The extraction mechanism is a three-step process: subject enrichment, relation propagation, and attribute extraction.
Approximately 70% of predictions use this extraction mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Projections to vocabulary space are an approximation, especially in early layers.
Attention knockout may have information leakage across positions, though blocking a range of layers alleviates this.
future_direction: knowledge localization
model editing
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) are known to capture factual knowledge in their parameters. While previous work looked into where factual associations are stored, only little is known about how they are retrieved internally during inference. We investigate this question through the lens of information flow. Given a subject-relation query, we study how the model aggregates information about the subject and relation to predict the correct attribute. With interventions on attention edges, we first identify two critical points where information propagates to the prediction: one from the relation positions followed by another from the subject positions. Next, by analyzing the information at these points, we unveil a three-step internal mechanism for attribute extraction. First, the representation at the last-subject position goes through an enrichment process, driven by the early MLP sublayers, to encode many subject-related attributes. Second, information from the relation propagates to the prediction. Third, the prediction representation "queries" the enriched subject to extract the attribute. Perhaps surprisingly, this extraction is typically done via attention heads, which often encode subject-attribute mappings in their parameters. Overall, our findings introduce a comprehensive view of how factual associations are stored and extracted internally in LMs, facilitating future research on knowledge localization and editing.

papers.title: A Graph Perspective to Probe Structural Patterns of Knowledge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do structural patterns of knowledge in large language models relate to graph properties, and can graph-based models predict knowledgeability to improve fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a graph-based approach to probe structural patterns of knowledge in LLMs, discovers novel patterns like knowledge homophily and correlation with node degree, and uses graph learning to predict knowledgeability for selecting informative triplets, leading to improved fine-tuning performance.
papers.conclusion: This work introduces a graph perspective to quantify and analyze structural patterns of knowledge in LLMs, revealing correlations with graph properties and homophily, and demonstrates the utility of graph learning for predicting knowledgeability and guiding effective fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Entity knowledgeability scores show a trimodal distribution (0, 0.5, 1) with domain-specific variation; temporal information reduces knowledgeability.
High homophily exists: topologically close entities have similar knowledgeability scores; temporal information reduces homophily.
Positive correlation between entity degree and knowledgeability: higher-degree entities tend to be better known.
GNN-based regression models outperform MLPs in predicting entity knowledgeability, and performance correlates with graph homophily.
Fine-tuning LLMs on triplets selected via predicted low knowledgeability (Graph-FT) outperforms random selection (Random-FT).
papers.limitation:
The derived structural patterns are used solely to guide triplet selection for fine-tuning, but they hold broader potential for applications like knowledge graph retrieval and identifying knowledge deficiency.
The approach is limited to knowledge graphs with explicitly defined entities and relations, and extending it to text-attributed graphs would broaden real-world applications.
future_direction: Extend the use of structural patterns to inform knowledge graph retrieval by identifying poor knowledge regions.
Apply the technique to efficiently identify knowledge deficiency through structural correlations.
Extend entity/triplet-level knowledgeability estimation to text-attributed graphs.
papers.abstract: Large language models have been extensively studied as neural knowledge bases for their knowledge access, editability, reasoning, and explainability. However, few works focus on the structural patterns of their knowledge. Motivated by this gap, we investigate these structural patterns from a graph perspective. We quantify the knowledge of LLMs at both the triplet and entity levels, and analyze how it relates to graph structural properties such as node degree. Furthermore, we uncover the knowledge homophily, where topologically close entities exhibit similar levels of knowledgeability, which further motivates us to develop graph machine learning models to estimate entity knowledge based on its local neighbors. This model further enables valuable knowledge checking by selecting triplets less known to LLMs. Empirical results show that using selected triplets for fine-tuning leads to superior performance.

papers.title: Locating and Extracting Relational Concepts in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are relational concepts represented within large language models, and can they be located and extracted?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that hidden states in shallow layers at the last token position solely express relational concepts, and demonstrates that these relational representations can be extracted and used for zero-shot relational reasoning and controllable fact recall via relation rewriting.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that relational representations can be located and extracted from LLMs, are faithful and robust, and can be used to control model responses, providing a stepping stone towards understanding the internal knowledge system of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden states at the last token position in shallow layers (the 'Relational Emergence stage') exclusively manifest the causal effects of relations, without subject information.
These relational representations can be accurately located and transplanted to other fact-recall processes, enabling the recall of new objects.
Extracted relational representations are faithful and robust entity connectors, enabling zero-shot relational reasoning with accuracy comparable to full-prompt prompting.
Relational representations can be used for controllable fact recall via 'relation rewriting', guiding model outputs to align with a desired relation without parameter modification.
The three-stage observation (Initial, Relational Emergence, Conjoint Influence) for locating relational representations does not hold for linguistic tasks (e.g., past tense prediction), limiting the method's applicability.
papers.limitation: The three-stage observation for locating relational representations is uncommon in fact recall processes involving linguistics (e.g., predicting past tense), where subject causal effects emerge before relations, limiting the method to non-linguistic relation location and extraction.
future_direction: Future research on how attention allocation is related to the causal effects of subjects and relations.
papers.abstract: Relational concepts are indeed foundational to the structure of knowledge representation, as they facilitate the association between various entity concepts, allowing us to express and comprehend complex world knowledge. By expressing relational concepts in natural language prompts, people can effortlessly interact with large language models (LLMs) and recall desired factual knowledge. However, the process of knowledge recall lacks interpretability, and representations of relational concepts within LLMs remain unknown to us. In this paper, we identify hidden states that can express entity and relational concepts through causal mediation analysis in fact recall processes. Our finding reveals that at the last token position of the input prompt, there are hidden states that solely express the causal effects of relational concepts. Based on this finding, we assume that these hidden states can be treated as relational representations and we can successfully extract them from LLMs. The experimental results demonstrate high credibility of the relational representations: they can be flexibly transplanted into other fact recall processes, and can also be used as robust entity connectors. Moreover, we also show that the relational representations exhibit significant potential for controllable fact recall through relation rewriting.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: Probing Cross-Modal Representations in Multi-Step Relational Reasoning
papers.research_question: What representations do vision and language models learn for multi-step relational reasoning, and can they generalize to novel synthetic data?
papers.core_contribution: Pretrained multimodal transformer-based architectures can perform higher-level relational reasoning and learn representations for novel tasks and synthetic data, with attention heads specializing in key objects and representations encoding threshold functions.
papers.conclusion: Transformer-based architectures pretrained on natural images can generalize to synthetic datasets and perform multi-step relational reasoning, with representations that encode contextual size and scene configuration.
papers.key_findings:
LXMERT achieves 88.8% accuracy on the multi-step relational reasoning task.
Most errors occur when the target object's size is close to the threshold, indicating the model learns the threshold function.
Different attention heads specialize in attending to the target, smallest, and biggest objects in the images.
Cross-modal representations encode the threshold function, as shown by linear regression predicting threshold values.
A diagnostic classifier can identify the odd-one-out image in a scene with high accuracy, indicating the model reasons over the scene.
papers.limitation: The findings are limited to synthetic data and one model; generalization to natural data and other models is left for future work.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other vision and language transformers and natural multimodal data.
papers.abstract: We investigate the representations learned by vision and language models in tasks that require relational reasoning. Focusing on the problem of assessing the relative size of objects in abstract visual contexts, we analyse both one-step and two-step reasoning. For the latter, we construct a new dataset of threeimage scenes and define a task that requires reasoning at the level of the individual images and across images in a scene. We probe the learned model representations using diagnostic classifiers. Our experiments show that pretrained multimodal transformer-based architectures can perform higher-level relational reasoning, and are able to learn representations for novel tasks and data that are very different from what was seen in pretraining.

papers.title: From Chains to DAGs: Probing the Graph Structure of Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the internal representation of LLMs encode graph-structured reasoning (as directed acyclic graphs) beyond linear chains, and where does this structure emerge across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Reasoning DAG Probing, a framework to test whether LLM hidden states linearly encode reasoning DAG structure, and finds that such structure is meaningfully encoded, peaking in intermediate layers, and varies with node depth, edge span, and model scale.
papers.conclusion: LLM reasoning is not purely sequential, but exhibits measurable internal graph structure.
papers.key_findings:
DAG structure is meaningfully encoded in LLM representations.
Recoverability of DAG structure peaks in intermediate layers.
Recovery varies systematically by node depth, edge span, and model scale.
The framework enables nontrivial recovery of dependency graphs.
Larger models achieve higher recoverability, and reasoning-oriented training recipes provide modest gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on frozen pretrained models; it remains open whether fine-tuning or reinforcement learning alters the internal geometry of reasoning.
The probing approach assumes that reasoning DAG structure is linearly accessible in hidden states; nonlinear or distributed encodings may require more expressive probes.
The DAG formalization for GSM8K relies on GPT-5 mini, which may introduce noise or bias.
future_direction: Extend the framework to dynamic or cyclic reasoning.
Incorporate more expressive probes.
Investigate how training interventions affect internal reasoning structure.
papers.abstract: Recent progress in large language models has renewed interest in mechanistically characterizing how multi-step reasoning is represented and computed. While much prior work treats reasoning as a linear chain of steps, many reasoning problems are more naturally structured as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where intermediate conclusions may depend on multiple premises, branch into parallel sub-derivations, and later merge or be reused. Understanding whether such graph-structured reasoning is reflected in model internals remains an open question. In this work, we introduce Reasoning DAG Probing, a framework that directly asks whether LLM hidden states encode the geometry of a reasoning DAG in a linearly accessible form, and where this structure emerges across layers. Within this framework, we associate each reasoning node with a textual realization and train lightweight probes to predict two graph-theoretic properties from hidden states: node depth and pairwise node distance. We use these probes to analyze the layerwise emergence of DAG structure and evaluate controls that disrupt reasoning-relevant structure while preserving superficial textual properties. Our results provide evidence that reasoning DAG geometry is meaningfully encoded in intermediate layers, with recoverability varying systematically by node depth and model scale, suggesting that LLM reasoning is not only sequential but exhibits measurable internal graph structure.

papers.title: Large Language Models Can Better Understand Knowledge Graphs Than We Thought
papers.research_question: Which input format of knowledge graphs (linearized triples vs. natural language text) is more effective for prompting LLMs to answer fact-intensive questions, and what are the underlying mechanisms and robustness implications?
papers.core_contribution: Linearized triples are more effective than natural language text for prompting LLMs on fact-intensive questions, and larger models are more susceptible to noisy or incomplete knowledge graphs.
papers.conclusion: Linearized triples are more effective for prompting LLMs on fact-intensive questions, and when designing prompt strategies for larger LLMs, the impact of noise in the subgraph should be considered.
papers.key_findings:
When using external knowledge to answer fact-intensive questions, LLMs prefer unordered structural data (linearized triples) over fluent NL text.
Sorting unordered linearized triples may not be necessary, as different LLMs prefer different prompt strategies; researchers need to conduct meticulous experiments to develop more universal KG knowledge injection prompts.
In the input format of linearized triples, LLMs with larger parameters are less robust to such inputs, i.e., they are more susceptible to noisy or incomplete KGs, resulting in performance degradation.
papers.abstract: When we integrate factual knowledge from knowledge graphs (KGs) into large language models (LLMs) to enhance their performance, the cost of injection through training increases with the scale of the models. Consequently, there is significant interest in developing prompt strategies that effectively incorporate KG information into LLMs. However, the community has not yet comprehensively understood how LLMs process and interpret KG information in different input formats and organizations within prompts, and researchers often rely on trial and error. To address this gap, we design extensive experiments to empirically study LLMs' comprehension of different KG prompts. At the literal level, we reveal LLMs' preferences for various input formats (from linearized triples to fluent natural language text). At the attention distribution level, we discuss the underlying mechanisms driving these preferences. We then investigate how the organization of structured knowledge impacts LLMs and evaluate LLMs' robustness in processing and utilizing KG information in practical scenarios. Our experiments show that (1) linearized triples are more effective than fluent NL text in helping LLMs understand KG information and answer fact-intensive questions; (2) Different LLMs exhibit varying preferences for different organizational formats of triples; (3) LLMs with larger scales are more susceptible to noisy, incomplete subgraphs.

papers.title: Identifying Linear Relational Concepts in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we identify human-interpretable concepts as directions in the latent space of hidden activations in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces linear relational concepts (LRC), a method that inverts linear relational embeddings (LRE) to find concept directions in hidden activations, extending LREs to multi-token objects and non-terminal layers, and outperforming standard probing classifiers in classification accuracy and causality.
papers.conclusion: Identifying and classifying human-interpretable concepts in language model activations is a vital step towards understanding language models. The linear relational concepts (LRC) technique outperforms standard linear classifiers on both classification accuracy and causality.
papers.key_findings:
LRCs outperform standard linear classifiers (SVM) and input averaging in both classification accuracy and causality.
Using earlier object layers for the LRE improves performance, especially for multi-token objects.
Using a low-rank pseudo-inverse of the LRE weight matrix improves performance, with optimal rank around 200 for Llama2-7b.
Training the LRE with samples from different objects in the same relation yields better LRCs than using samples from the same object.
There is a trade-off between causality and classification accuracy depending on the subject layer: earlier layers yield higher causality but lower classification accuracy.
papers.limitation:
The method requires learning a new LRC for every (relation, object) pair and cannot generalize to new objects without a training sample.
The evaluation assumes each subject maps to a single object in the same relation and cannot handle subjects with multiple objects.
The method assumes that if the model outputs the correct answer, it has a representation of the concept, but the model might guess correctly without an underlying representation.
The method assumes knowledge is in the subject token residual stream, but recent work suggests some knowledge may be contained in attention values and added to the output token residual stream.
The method works only for relational concepts of the form (subject, relation, object).
future_direction: Optimizing the LRE training samples chosen for each LRC.
Combining LRCs learned at multiple layers to improve both classification accuracy and causality.
Investigating relations between concepts within model weights and extracting knowledge or world models directly from pretrained language models.
papers.abstract: Transformer language models (LMs) have been shown to represent concepts as directions in the latent space of hidden activations. However, for any human-interpretable concept, how can we find its direction in the latent space? We present a technique called linear relational concepts (LRC) for finding concept directions corresponding to human-interpretable concepts by first modeling the relation between subject and object as a linear relational embedding (LRE). We find that inverting the LRE and using earlier object layers results in a powerful technique for finding concept directions that outperforms standard black-box probing classifiers. We evaluate LRCs on their performance as concept classifiers as well as their ability to causally change model output.

papers.title: Memorization, Emergence, and Explaining Reversal Failures: A Controlled Study of Relational Semantics in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether autoregressive LLMs learn the logical semantics of relational words (e.g., symmetry and inversion) and whether reversal-type failures arise from missing relational semantics or left-to-right order bias.
papers.core_contribution: Relational semantics emerge with sufficient logic-bearing supervision, enabling generalization to unseen entities, and reversal failures are primarily driven by autoregressive order bias rather than deficient inversion semantics.
papers.conclusion: Autoregressive LMs can learn relational word logical semantics with sufficient supervision, and reversal failures are due to order bias, not semantic deficiencies.
papers.key_findings:
Autoregressive LMs can memorize relational facts during pre-training and answer both memorize and logic questions in forward order.
Relational semantics emerge with sufficient logic-bearing supervision, exhibiting a sharp phase transition as training data increases, even in shallow models.
Successful relational generalization is associated with stable, logic-relevant representations in intermediate layers.
Reversal-type failures primarily stem from order bias in left-to-right autoregressive decoding, not missing relational semantics, and are mitigated by bidirectional data exposure.
papers.limitation:
Limited relational word types, focusing only on symmetric and inverse relations, not broader semantics like transitivity or multi-hop rules.
Template-based language generation may not reflect natural text variation.
Diffusion LM training is not fully mature for comprehensive comparison.
ICL evaluation may involve shallow matching rather than pure relational understanding.
Limited pretrained-model evaluation, not covering forward-reverse gaps in pretrained settings.
future_direction: Extending to more complex relational properties like transitivity or compositional rules.
Improving diffusion LM training for accurate comparison with autoregressive models.
Evaluating reversal failures in pretrained models more comprehensively.
papers.abstract: Autoregressive LLMs perform well on relational tasks that require linking entities via relational words (e.g., father/son, friend), but it is unclear whether they learn the logical semantics of such relations (e.g., symmetry and inversion logic) and, if so, whether reversal-type failures arise from missing relational semantics or left-to-right order bias. We propose a controlled Knowledge Graph-based synthetic framework that generates text from symmetric/inverse triples, train GPT-style autoregressive models from scratch, and evaluate memorization, logical inference, and in-context generalization to unseen entities to address these questions. We find a sharp phase transition in which relational semantics emerge with sufficient logic-bearing supervision, even in shallow (2-3 layer) models, and that successful generalization aligns with stable intermediate-layer signals. Finally, order-matched forward/reverse tests and a diffusion baseline indicate that reversal failures are primarily driven by autoregressive order bias rather than deficient inversion semantics.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Bilinear relational structure fixes reversal curse and enables consistent model editing
papers.research_question: Is the reversal curse an inherent limitation of language models, and can it be mitigated by learning a bilinear relational structure in internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The reversal curse and model editing failures are not inherent but stem from unstructured knowledge representations; training with appropriate regularization induces a bilinear relational structure that mitigates the curse and enables logically consistent editing.
papers.conclusion: The reversal curse and editing generalization failures are symptoms of unstructured internal knowledge representations; inducing bilinear relational geometry through training and regularization leads to more reliable and editable language models.
papers.key_findings:
Weight decay regularization enables models to overcome the reversal curse by learning a more generalizable internal structure.
Successful models develop a robust bilinear relational structure in their hidden representations, peaking in middle layers.
The learned bilinear matrices obey algebraic properties (inversion via transpose, composition via product), enabling multi-hop inference.
Models with bilinear structure successfully propagate single-fact edits to logically entailed facts (reverse and neighborhood relations).
A strong positive correlation exists between a model's bilinear probe accuracy and its logical generalization performance after editing.
papers.limitation: The study uses language models trained from scratch on a clean, synthetic dataset, which may not scale to large, pre-trained language models with noisy, complex knowledge.
future_direction: Investigate whether similar bilinear structures exist in large-scale pre-trained language models.
Develop geometry-aware editing algorithms that leverage internal relational structures.
Explore 'architectural preparation' strategies to endow models with structured knowledge representations during pre-training or fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The reversal curse -- a language model's (LM) inability to infer an unseen fact ``B is A'' from a learned fact ``A is B'' -- is widely considered a fundamental limitation. We show that this is not an inherent failure but an artifact of how models encode knowledge. By training LMs from scratch on a synthetic dataset of relational knowledge graphs, we demonstrate that bilinear relational structure emerges in their hidden representations. This structure substantially alleviates the reversal curse, enabling LMs to infer unseen reverse facts. Crucially, we also find that this bilinear structure plays a key role in consistent model editing. When a fact is updated in a LM with this structure, the edit correctly propagates to its reverse and other logically dependent facts. In contrast, models lacking this representation not only suffer from the reversal curse but also fail to generalize edits, further introducing logical inconsistencies. Our results establish that training on a relational knowledge dataset induces the emergence of bilinear internal representations, which in turn enable LMs to behave in a logically consistent manner after editing. This implies that the success of model editing depends critically not just on editing algorithms but on the underlying representational geometry of the knowledge being modified.

papers.title: The Structure of Relation Decoding Linear Operators in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What underlying regularities or shared structures allow the affine relational decoders to be compressed, and how are they organized in transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear relation decoders in LLMs are highly compressible via order-3 tensor networks and are organized around coarse-grained semantic properties rather than being relation-specific.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that relation decoders in transformer language models are property-based and compressible, organizing into common properties recurring across relations rather than being isolated mappings.
papers.key_findings:
Relation decoding matrices are highly compressible using order-3 tensor networks with minimal loss in faithfulness.
Cross-evaluation reveals that decoders are not relation-specific but extract recurring semantic properties (e.g., country, gender).
The property-centric structure explains compressibility and limited generalization to semantically close relations.
Tensor networks achieve good sample-wise generalization on the original dataset but limited relation-wise generalization on general language data.
On mathematical datasets, tensor networks achieve near-perfect generalization.
papers.limitation: The study relies on linear approximations extracted from relatively small language models (with 6, 8, and 20 billion parameters) and a biased subset of relations, so generalization to larger models and the full space of relations is unclear.
future_direction: Improving generalization of tensor network models on general language data.
Applying the tensor network framework to low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and mixture-of-experts models.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the structure of linear operators introduced in Hernandez et al. [2023] that decode specific relational facts in transformer language models. We extend their single-relation findings to a collection of relations and systematically chart their organization. We show that such collections of relation decoders can be highly compressed by simple order-3 tensor networks without significant loss in decoding accuracy. To explain this surprising redundancy, we develop a cross-evaluation protocol, in which we apply each linear decoder operator to the subjects of every other relation. Our results reveal that these linear maps do not encode distinct relations, but extract recurring, coarse-grained semantic properties (e.g., country of capital city and country of food are both in the country-of-X property). This property-centric structure clarifies both the operators' compressibility and highlights why they generalize only to new relations that are semantically close. Our findings thus interpret linear relational decoding in transformer language models as primarily property-based, rather than relation-specific.

papers.title: Relational Schemata in BERT Are Inducible, Not Emergent: A Study of Performance vs. Competence in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does BERT encode abstract relational schemata, and is relational abstraction emergent from pretraining or induced via task scaffolding?
papers.core_contribution: Relational schemata in BERT are not emergent from pretraining but can be induced through task-specific fine-tuning, revealing a performance-competence gap where high classification accuracy does not imply structured internal representations.
papers.conclusion: This study demonstrates a clear separation between performance and competence in BERT's handling of relational reasoning. Relational abstraction is not an emergent property of pretraining but must be actively induced through guided learning.
papers.key_findings:
Pretrained BERT achieves high accuracy (79%) on relation classification, but its internal representations do not show relational structure (low RSA correlation).
After fine-tuning, BERT's accuracy increases to 90% and its internal representations show strong relational structure (high RSA correlation and clustering in embedding space).
A performance-competence gap exists: BERT can perform well on relational tasks without having structured internal representations.
Relational abstraction is not emergent from pretraining but requires task-specific supervision to induce.
Control experiments with randomized labels confirm that classification success and RSA structure reflect genuine relational signals, not dataset artifacts.
future_direction: Explore whether similar patterns of inducibility extend to other language models (e.g., LLaMa, Gemma) and whether model scale influences the emergence of relational structure.
Extend the range of tested relations to include temporal or causal relations.
Bridge insights from cognitive development (e.g., curriculum learning, relational priming) to inspire new training paradigms.
papers.abstract: While large language models like BERT demonstrate strong empirical performance on semantic tasks, whether this reflects true conceptual competence or surface-level statistical association remains unclear. I investigate whether BERT encodes abstract relational schemata by examining internal representations of concept pairs across taxonomic, mereological, and functional relations. I compare BERT's relational classification performance with representational structure in [CLS] token embeddings. Results reveal that pretrained BERT enables high classification accuracy, indicating latent relational signals. However, concept pairs organize by relation type in high-dimensional embedding space only after fine-tuning on supervised relation classification tasks. This indicates relational schemata are not emergent from pretraining alone but can be induced via task scaffolding. These findings demonstrate that behavioral performance does not necessarily imply structured conceptual understanding, though models can acquire inductive biases for grounded relational abstraction through appropriate training.

papers.title: $R^2$-CoD: Understanding Text-Graph Complementarity in Relational Reasoning via Knowledge Co-Distillation
papers.research_question: How do text and graph representations relate to each other during learning in relational reasoning tasks, and under what conditions does their integration improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified framework (R2-CoD) to analyze text-graph representation complementarity in relational reasoning, revealing patterns of alignment and divergence shaped by task characteristics.
papers.conclusion: Text and graph representations show a spectrum of behaviors from alignment to complementarity in relational reasoning tasks, shaped by task structure such as token-node correspondence and reasoning scope, and CoD provides a useful framework for understanding and leveraging these relationships.
papers.key_findings:
Hybrid models with CoD generally outperform text-only or graph-only baselines across tasks.
Text and graph representations exhibit a spectrum from complementarity to alignment, with tasks like ETRE showing complementarity and tasks like FU showing alignment.
Tasks with one-to-one token-node correspondence (e.g., FU, KBQA) tend to show alignment, while those without such correspondence (e.g., ETRE) show complementarity.
The level of reasoning (global vs. local) affects alignment, as seen in RPP (global) vs. KBQA (local).
CoD is most beneficial when text and graph encode complementary information, as in ETRE and FU.
papers.limitation:
Task coverage is limited to five relational reasoning tasks; extending to other tasks may reveal additional behaviors.
Analysis relies on PCA and distance metrics, which may not capture all fine-grained or non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other tasks to reveal additional representational behaviors.
Use advanced probing or disentanglement techniques for finer-grained analysis.
papers.abstract: Relational reasoning lies at the core of many NLP tasks, drawing on complementary signals from text and graphs. While prior research has investigated how to leverage this dual complementarity, a detailed and systematic understanding of text-graph interplay and its effect on hybrid models remains underexplored. We take an analysis-driven approach to investigate text-graph representation complementarity via a unified architecture that supports knowledge co-distillation (CoD). We explore five tasks involving relational reasoning that differ in how text and graph structures encode the information needed to solve that task. By tracking how these dual representations evolve during training, we uncover interpretable patterns of alignment and divergence, and provide insights into when and why their integration is beneficial.

papers.title: Grounding LLM Reasoning with Knowledge Graphs
papers.research_question: How can grounding LLM reasoning in knowledge graphs improve accuracy and interpretability by linking each reasoning step to structured graph data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that grounds LLM reasoning in knowledge graphs by linking each reasoning step to graph data, improving both accuracy and interpretability on complex question-answering tasks.
papers.conclusion: Grounding LLM reasoning in knowledge graphs by integrating reasoning steps with structured retrieval improves accuracy and offers a more interpretable view of the reasoning process, suggesting a path toward systematic and transparent reasoning interventions.
papers.key_findings:
The agentic method for graph interaction generally outperforms automatic graph exploration, indicating targeted interventions enhance accuracy.
The Tree-of-Thought (ToT) reasoning strategy shows superior performance by exploring multiple reasoning paths.
Graph-of-Thought (GoT) does not outperform ToT, revealing challenges in merging divergent reasoning paths effectively.
Performance improves with more reasoning steps for agentic methods, while automatic exploration performs well with fewer steps.
The framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on GRBench, with at least 26.5% improvement over Chain-of-Thought baselines.
papers.limitation:
Computational complexity grows exponentially for Tree-of-Thought and Graph-of-Thought due to branching, limiting scalability.
Effectiveness depends on the coverage and quality of the underlying knowledge graph.
LLMs may still hallucinate despite grounding in graph structure.
