future_direction: Extending the framework to larger and more heterogeneous graphs.
Exploring how structured retrieval can guide reasoning in domains where accuracy and verifiability are critical.
Developing more advanced intervention strategies for merging partial reasoning outcomes.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at generating natural language answers, yet their outputs often remain unverifiable and difficult to trace. Knowledge Graphs (KGs) offer a complementary strength by representing entities and their relationships in structured form, providing a foundation for more reliable reasoning. We propose a novel framework that integrates LLM reasoning with KGs by linking each step of the reasoning process to graph-structured data. This grounding turns intermediate ``thoughts'' into interpretable traces that remain consistent with external knowledge. Our approach incorporates multiple reasoning strategies, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Tree-of-Thought (ToT), and Graph-of-Thought (GoT), and is evaluated on GRBench, a benchmark for domain-specific graph reasoning. Our experiments show state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, with at least 26.5\% improvement over CoT baselines. Beyond accuracy, we analyze how step depth, branching structure, and model size influence reasoning quality, offering insights into the conditions that support effective reasoning. Together, these contributions highlight how grounding LLMs in structured knowledge enables both higher accuracy and greater interpretability in complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Function Vectors for Relational Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether the framework of function vectors can be effectively extended to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to support interpretable and generalizable relational reasoning.
papers.core_contribution: This thesis extends the function vector framework to multimodal large language models, demonstrating that task-specific representations can be extracted from attention head activations and used to causally control relational reasoning in zero-shot settings.
papers.conclusion: Function vectors are flexible and transferable modules that can be used to control and enhance reasoning in MLLMs, validating their role as causally meaningful encodings of task-specific computations.
papers.key_findings:
Function vectors can be extracted from the activations of a sparse subset of attention heads in MLLMs and retain causal influence over the model's output.
The most causally influential heads for relational reasoning tend to reside in the model's mid-layers.
Injecting function vectors into zero-shot prompts significantly increases the model's ability to make correct relational predictions.
Fine-tuning function vectors on zero-shot examples yields substantial performance gains, surpassing few-shot in-context learning baselines.
Relational reasoning is driven by a sparse set of causally influential attention heads, and optimal performance is achieved with a small number of carefully selected heads.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted using a single, relatively lightweight architecture (OpenFlamingo-4B), and it remains to be seen whether the findings generalize to larger and more complex models.
The scope of relational tasks is restricted to a small set of synthetic spatial relations (e.g., above, next to), which does not capture the full richness of real-world relational reasoning.
The synthetic nature of the dataset may limit the ecological validity of the findings.
future_direction: Explore whether the function vector framework generalizes to larger, more advanced multimodal architectures.
Extend the analysis to a broader range of relational categories, including physical, agentic, and social relations.
Apply the method to real-world, naturalistic datasets to evaluate its practical utility.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit impressive relational reasoning abilities from limited examples, yet the internal mechanisms supporting such behavior remain opaque. This thesis proposes a causal framework for interpreting and controlling relational behavior in MLLMs by extracting and manipulating function vectors: task-specific representations computed from attention head activations. Extending previous work in language-only models, we demonstrate that function vectors can also be identified in the vision-language model OpenFlamingo-4B and used to induce relational behavior in zero-shot settings. Using a synthetic image dataset designed to isolate spatial relations, we apply causal mediation analysis to identify a small subset of attention heads with high influence on relational predictions. These heads define compact function vectors that, when injected into the model’s hidden states, significantly improve zero-shot accuracy. We further show that these vectors can be fine-tuned—while keeping model parameters fixed—to enhance generalization and outperform in-context learning baselines. Our results reveal that MLLMs encode relational functions within localized internal structures, which can be systematically interpreted and optimized, advancing our understanding of model modularity and control.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: The Geometry of Categorical and Hierarchical Concepts in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the linear representation hypothesis be extended to represent categorical and hierarchical concepts in large language models, and how are hierarchical relationships encoded geometrically in the representation space?
papers.core_contribution: Extends the linear representation hypothesis to represent binary features as vectors and categorical concepts as polytopes, and proves that hierarchical relationships between concepts are encoded as orthogonality in the representation space.
papers.conclusion: The representation space of large language models encodes hierarchical semantic structure through a simple direct sum of polytopes, where hierarchical relations correspond to orthogonality.
papers.key_findings:
Binary features can be represented as vectors in the transformed representation space, with words belonging to the feature having similar projections onto the vector.
Categorical concepts are represented as polytopes, where vertices correspond to vector representations of the concept's elements.
Hierarchical relationships (e.g., parent-child) are geometrically encoded as orthogonality between the corresponding vector representations.
Empirical validation on Gemma and LLaMA-3 models shows the estimated vector representations for WordNet concepts align with the semantic hierarchy, exhibiting the predicted orthogonal structure.
The canonical representation space (using a causal inner product) is necessary to observe the hierarchical orthogonality; it does not hold under the naive Euclidean inner product.
papers.limitation:
The analysis and whitening transformation are limited to the final layer representation; understanding the geometry of internal layers remains an open question.
Perfect linear representations as defined may not be found by gradient descent in practice; the theory assumes their existence.
future_direction: Extending the geometric analysis to the internal layers of language models.
Designing interpretability methods (e.g., sparse autoencoders) that explicitly account for the hierarchical structure of semantic concepts.
papers.abstract: The linear representation hypothesis is the informal idea that semantic concepts are encoded as linear directions in the representation spaces of large language models (LLMs). Previous work has shown how to make this notion precise for representing binary concepts that have natural contrasts (e.g., {male, female}) as directions in representation space. However, many natural concepts do not have natural contrasts (e.g., whether the output is about an animal). In this work, we show how to extend the formalization of the linear representation hypothesis to represent features (e.g., is_animal) as vectors. This allows us to immediately formalize the representation of categorical concepts as polytopes in the representation space. Further, we use the formalization to prove a relationship between the hierarchical structure of concepts and the geometry of their representations. We validate these theoretical results on the Gemma and LLaMA-3 large language models, estimating representations for 900+ hierarchically related concepts using data from WordNet.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Sparse Feature Coactivation Reveals Causal Semantic Modules in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can sparse feature coactivation be used to identify causal semantic modules in large language models, and how do these modules enable targeted manipulation of model outputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse feature coactivation can identify semantically coherent components in LLMs that causally influence model outputs, enabling precise steering and counterfactual generation through ablation and amplification.
papers.conclusion: The study supports a modular and compositional structure of knowledge in LLMs, and introduces an efficient method for causal interpretation and manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse feature coactivation identifies semantically coherent components for concepts and relations in LLMs.
Ablating or amplifying these components causally changes model outputs, enabling counterfactual steering.
Components can be composed to produce compound counterfactual outputs.
Concept components tend to emerge in early layers, while relation components are concentrated in later layers.
Extracted components provide a more comprehensive and specific account than individual SAE features.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on pretrained sparse autoencoders, which may not be available for all models.
Results primarily limited to Gemma 2 2B, with limited validation on other models.
Focus only on sparsely activating features, ignoring high-density features that may have important functions.
future_direction: Expand the method to more models and tasks.
Investigate the role of high-density features.
Explore applications to hierarchical knowledge tasks.
papers.abstract: We identify semantically coherent, context-consistent network components in large language models (LLMs) using coactivation of sparse autoencoder (SAE) features collected from just a handful of prompts. Focusing on concept-relation prediction tasks, we show that ablating these components for concepts (e.g., countries and words) and relations (e.g., capital city and translation language) changes model outputs in predictable ways, while amplifying these components induces counterfactual responses. Notably, composing relation and concept components yields compound counterfactual outputs. Further analysis reveals that while most concept components emerge from the very first layer, more abstract relation components are concentrated in later layers. Lastly, we show that extracted components more comprehensively capture concepts and relations than individual features while maintaining specificity. Overall, our findings suggest a modular organization of knowledge accessed through compositional operations, and advance methods for efficient, targeted LLM manipulation.

papers.title: The Representational Geometry of Number
papers.research_question: How do number representations in language models maintain a stable relational structure across different tasks, and how are task-specific subspaces related?
papers.core_contribution: Number representations in language models preserve a stable relational structure across tasks, with task-specific subspaces that are largely transformable via linear mappings, balancing shared structure and functional flexibility.
papers.conclusion: The representational geometry of numbers in LLMs reveals a shared relational structure that supports task flexibility through linear transformations, unifying previous theories and extending beyond number concepts.
papers.key_findings:
Number embeddings maintain a consistent sequential order across tasks, as visualized with t-SNE.
Distance, size, and ratio effects are preserved across tasks, indicating human-like magnitude encoding.
Low-level features like parity and magnitude are encoded in separable linear directions, with parity nearly orthogonal to magnitude.
Task-specific representations occupy distinct subspaces with low overlap but high canonical correlation, showing they are related by linear transformations.
The relational structure is shared across models and formats, as shown by low Procrustes disparity.
papers.abstract: A central question in cognitive science is whether conceptual representations converge onto a shared manifold to support generalization, or diverge into orthogonal subspaces to minimize task interference. While prior work has discovered evidence for both, a mechanistic account of how these properties coexist and transform across tasks remains elusive. We propose that representational sharing lies not in the concepts themselves, but in the geometric relations between them. Using number concepts as a testbed and language models as high-dimensional computational substrates, we show that number representations preserve a stable relational structure across tasks. Task-specific representations are embedded in distinct subspaces, with low-level features like magnitude and parity encoded along separable linear directions. Crucially, we find that these subspaces are largely transformable into one another via linear mappings, indicating that representations share relational structure despite being located in distinct subspaces. Together, these results provide a mechanistic lens of how language models balance the shared structure of number representation with functional flexibility. It suggests that understanding arises when task-specific transformations are applied to a shared underlying relational structure of conceptual representations.

papers.title: On Relation-Specific Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do relation-specific neurons exist in large language models, i.e., neurons that focus on a relation itself independent of any entity, and what are their properties?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates the existence of relation-specific neurons in LLMs and provides evidence for their properties: cumulativity, versatility, and interference.
papers.conclusion: Relation-specific neurons exist in LLMs and exhibit properties of cumulativity, versatility, and interference, indicating distributed and overlapping encoding of relational knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Relation-specific neurons exist in LLMs and are located primarily in the middle layers.
Neuron cumulativity: Multiple neurons jointly contribute to processing facts involving a relation, with no single neuron fully encoding a fact.
Neuron versatility: Neurons can be shared across multiple closely related as well as less related relations, and some transfer across languages.
Neuron interference: Deactivating neurons specific to one relation can improve LLMs' factual recall performance for facts of other relations.
The effect of deactivating relation-specific neurons is more pronounced when more neurons are deactivated, and the neurons are effective across different prompt templates and languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a set of 12 relations and two model families (LLama-2 and Gemma).
future_direction: Extend analysis to more relations and model families.
Investigate the dynamics of relation-specific neurons during training.
Explore whether similar neurons exist for other types of knowledge or tasks.
papers.abstract: In large language models (LLMs), certain \emph{neurons} can store distinct pieces of knowledge learned during pretraining. While factual knowledge typically appears as a combination of \emph{relations} and \emph{entities}, it remains unclear whether some neurons focus on a relation itself -- independent of any entity. We hypothesize such neurons \emph{detect} a relation in the input text and \emph{guide} generation involving such a relation. To investigate this, we study the LLama-2 family on a chosen set of relations, with a \textit{statistics}-based method. Our experiments demonstrate the existence of relation-specific neurons. We measure the effect of selectively deactivating candidate neurons specific to relation $r$ on the LLM's ability to handle (1) facts involving relation $r$ and (2) facts involving a different relation $r' \neq r$. With respect to their capacity for encoding relation information, we give evidence for the following three properties of relation-specific neurons. \textbf{(i) Neuron cumulativity.} Multiple neurons jointly contribute to processing facts involving relation $r$, with no single neuron fully encoding a fact in $r$ on its own. \textbf{(ii) Neuron versatility.} Neurons can be shared across multiple closely related as well as less related relations. In addition, some relation neurons transfer across languages. \textbf{(iii) Neuron interference.} Deactivating neurons specific to one relation can improve LLMs' factual recall performance for facts of other relations. We make our code and data publicly available at https://github.com/cisnlp/relation-specific-neurons.

papers.title: From Latent to Lucid: Transforming Knowledge Graph Embeddings into Interpretable Structures with KGEPrisma
papers.research_question: How can we provide faithful and interpretable post-hoc explanations for Knowledge Graph Embedding models by decoding their latent representations into symbolic structures?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KGEPrisma, a post-hoc and local explainable AI method for Knowledge Graph Embedding models that decodes their latent representations into interpretable symbolic rules and facts without retraining, providing faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: KGEPrisma effectively bridges the gap between the abstract latent representations of KGE models and interpretable symbolic explanations, enhancing transparency and trustworthiness.
papers.key_findings:
KGEPrisma outperforms state-of-the-art methods (AnyBURLExplainer, Data Poisoning, Kelpie) in faithfulness on FB15k-237 and WN18RR.
The method is effective across different KGE models (TransE, DistMult, ConvE).
It provides three types of explanations: rule-based, instance-based, and analogy-based.
The method is computationally efficient as it does not require retraining.
KGEPrisma's explanations are faithful and well-localized to the model's decision surface.
future_direction: Apply KGEPrisma to biomedical knowledge graphs to improve decision-making and trust.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a post-hoc and local explainable AI method tailored for Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) models. These models are essential to Knowledge Graph Completion yet criticized for their opaque, black-box nature. Despite their significant success in capturing the semantics of knowledge graphs through high-dimensional latent representations, their inherent complexity poses substantial challenges to explainability. While existing methods like Kelpie use resource-intensive perturbation to explain KGE models, our approach directly decodes the latent representations encoded by KGE models, leveraging the smoothness of the embeddings, which follows the principle that similar embeddings reflect similar behaviours within the Knowledge Graph, meaning that nodes are similarly embedded because their graph neighbourhood looks similar. This principle is commonly referred to as smoothness. By identifying symbolic structures, in the form of triples, within the subgraph neighborhoods of similarly embedded entities, our method identifies the statistical regularities on which the models rely and translates these insights into human-understandable symbolic rules and facts. This bridges the gap between the abstract representations of KGE models and their predictive outputs, offering clear, interpretable insights. Key contributions include a novel post-hoc and local explainable AI method for KGE models that provides immediate, faithful explanations without retraining, facilitating real-time application on large-scale knowledge graphs. The method's flexibility enables the generation of rule-based, instance-based, and analogy-based explanations, meeting diverse user needs. Extensive evaluations show the effectiveness of our approach in delivering faithful and well-localized explanations, enhancing the transparency and trustworthiness of KGE models.

papers.title: LLM Interpretability with Identifiable Temporal-Instantaneous Representation
papers.research_question: How can we learn interpretable temporal and instantaneous causal representations from LLM activations with theoretical guarantees?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a temporal causal representation learning framework for LLM interpretability that captures time-delayed and instantaneous causal relations with theoretical guarantees.
papers.conclusion: The proposed temporal causal representation learning framework provides a principled way to uncover temporal and instantaneous causal structures in LLM activations, offering a step toward more interpretable and controllable language models.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully discovers meaningful concept relationships in LLM activations by extending sparse autoencoder techniques.
Modeling both temporal and instantaneous conceptual relationships advances the interpretability of LLMs.
The method provides theoretical guarantees for identifiability under linear assumptions and sparsity constraints.
It demonstrates efficacy on synthetic datasets scaled to real-world complexity and on activations from real LLMs.
The approach offers a principled way to uncover causal structures in LLM activations.
papers.limitation: The linearity assumption may not hold in practice, and the scalability to very high-dimensional spaces is limited by the need to estimate large matrices.
future_direction: Extending the framework to nonlinear models.
Scaling the approach to larger models and higher-dimensional spaces.
Incorporating domain knowledge to guide the discovery of causal structures.
papers.abstract: Despite Large Language Models' remarkable capabilities, understanding their internal representations remains challenging. Mechanistic interpretability tools such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs) were developed to extract interpretable features from LLMs but lack temporal dependency modeling, instantaneous relation representation, and more importantly theoretical guarantees, undermining both the theoretical foundations and the practical confidence necessary for subsequent analyses. While causal representation learning (CRL) offers theoretically grounded approaches for uncovering latent concepts, existing methods cannot scale to LLMs' rich conceptual space due to inefficient computation. To bridge the gap, we introduce an identifiable temporal causal representation learning framework specifically designed for LLMs' high-dimensional concept space, capturing both time-delayed and instantaneous causal relations. Our approach provides theoretical guarantees and demonstrates efficacy on synthetic datasets scaled to match real-world complexity. By extending SAE techniques with our temporal causal framework, we successfully discover meaningful concept relationships in LLM activations. Our findings show that modeling both temporal and instantaneous conceptual relationships advances the interpretability of LLMs.

papers.title: Large language models converge toward human-like concept organization
papers.research_question: Do large language models create rich concept-based mental models central to human understanding, and does scaling these models create even better concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that the vector spaces of larger and better language models become increasingly structurally similar to those of knowledge graph embeddings, indicating that LLMs converge toward human-like concept organization and induce implicit models of world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Large language models converge toward human-like concept organization, building implicit models of the world, which has important practical and philosophical implications.
papers.key_findings:
Larger language models within each family lead to better alignments with the reference vector spaces from knowledge graph embeddings.
The convergence trend is robust across four language model families (OPT, GPT-2/3, Pythia, BERT) and three graph embedding systems (BigGraph, TransE, ComplEx).
Performance in alignment is affected by polysemy and semantic category, with monosemous words and certain categories (like places) showing better convergence.
GPT models exhibit the most pronounced convergence properties and achieve the best overall results on the analogy task.
The results suggest that language models induce inferential semantics, partially settling the debate about their capacity for understanding.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to English; language characteristics and morpho-syntactic properties may influence how corpora and knowledge bases align.
Only three families of autoregressive language models and one non-autoregressive family were compared.
The set of variables that covary with performance is probably much larger than the polysemy and semantic categories analyzed.
future_direction: Investigating why for some models, words with two to three meanings result in better performance.
Exploring how language characteristics affect the quality of word vector spaces.
Examining a broader set of variables that may covary with alignment performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models show human-like performance in knowledge extraction, reasoning and dialogue, but it remains controversial whether this performance is best explained by memorization and pattern matching, or whether it reflects human-like inferential semantics and world knowledge. Knowledge bases such as WikiData provide large-scale, high-quality representations of inferential semantics and world knowledge. We show that large language models learn to organize concepts in ways that are strikingly similar to how concepts are organized in such knowledge bases. Knowledge bases model collective, institutional knowledge, and large language models seem to induce such knowledge from raw text. We show that bigger and better models exhibit more human-like concept organization, across four families of language models and three knowledge graph embeddings.

papers.title: A Geometric Notion of Causal Probing
papers.research_question: How can we define an intrinsic, information-theoretic measure of concept information in linear subspaces of language model representations, and how can this enable causal probing and controlled generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an intrinsic, information-theoretic framework for measuring concept information in linear subspaces of language model representations, accounting for spurious correlations, and proposes a causal graphical model for controlled generation via do-interventions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed geometric framework provides an intrinsic way to measure concept information in language model representations and enables causal controlled generation, though with limitations due to computational intractability and model assumptions.
papers.key_findings:
LEACE yields a representation space partitioning that partially meets the counterfactual criteria for erasure and encapsulation.
The do-intervention for controlled generation is effective for verbal-number in GPT2 and Llama 2 but not for grammatical-gender.
The framework reconciles statistical concept information with geometric encoding, enabling causal interpretation of concept subspaces.
The counterfactual metrics are optimized by the true causal subspace when it exists, but the objective is computationally intractable.
The method improves upon INLP and LEACE as causal effect estimators on the CEBaB benchmark.
papers.limitation: The counterfactual objective for identifying the concept subspace is computationally intractable due to nested sums over the infinite representation space.
future_direction: Developing a tractable approximation for the counterfactual objective.
Extending the framework to more concepts and models.
Further exploration of the causal assumptions and their practical implications.
papers.abstract: The linear subspace hypothesis (Bolukbasi et al., 2016) states that, in a language model's representation space, all information about a concept such as verbal number is encoded in a linear subspace. Prior work has relied on auxiliary classification tasks to identify and evaluate candidate subspaces that might give support for this hypothesis. We instead give a set of intrinsic criteria which characterize an ideal linear concept subspace and enable us to identify the subspace using only the language model distribution. Our information-theoretic framework accounts for spuriously correlated features in the representation space (Kumar et al., 2022) by reconciling the statistical notion of concept information and the geometric notion of how concepts are encoded in the representation space. As a byproduct of this analysis, we hypothesize a causal process for how a language model might leverage concepts during generation. Empirically, we find that linear concept erasure is successful in erasing most concept information under our framework for verbal number as well as some complex aspect-level sentiment concepts from a restaurant review dataset. Our causal intervention for controlled generation shows that, for at least one concept across two languages models, the concept subspace can be used to manipulate the concept value of the generated word with precision.

papers.title: Multimodal Function Vectors for Spatial Relations
papers.research_question: Whether the concept of function vectors can be extended from language-only transformer models to large multimodal models (LMMs) to support the extraction and manipulation of relational knowledge in images, and how architectural factors influence the effectiveness of function vector interventions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that spatial relational knowledge in a vision-language model is encoded within a sparse subset of attention heads and can be extracted as 'multimodal function vectors'. These vectors can be fine-tuned and linearly combined to solve novel relational tasks, advancing understanding of model modularity and control over relational reasoning in LMMs.
papers.conclusion: The results confirm that function vectors can be extracted from LMMs, encode causally meaningful relational knowledge, and serve as flexible, optimizable modules that can be combined to enhance and control relational reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset of attention heads in OpenFlamingo-4B is causally responsible for transmitting representations of spatial relations.
Extracted relation-specific function vectors, when injected into zero-shot prompts, significantly improve relational prediction accuracy.
Fine-tuning these function vectors with a modest amount of data while keeping the LMM frozen outperforms few-shot in-context learning baselines.
Relation-specific function vectors can be linearly combined to form composite vectors that solve one-shot analogy problems involving novel, untrained spatial relations.
The effectiveness of function vector intervention depends on the injection layer and the number of heads used, peaking at intermediate layers and a small subset of heads.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted using a single, relatively lightweight architecture (OpenFlamingo-4B), and it remains to be seen whether findings generalize to larger, more complex models.
The scope of relational tasks investigated is restricted to a small set of spatial relations (e.g., above, next to), not capturing the full richness of real-world multimodal tasks.
future_direction: Explore whether the multimodal function vector framework generalizes to larger, more advanced multimodal architectures with different training regimes and fusion mechanisms.
Extend the analysis to a broader range of relational categories, including physical, agentic, and social relations.
papers.abstract: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) demonstrate impressive in-context learning abilities from limited multimodal demonstrations, yet the internal mechanisms supporting such task learning remain opaque. Building on prior work of large language models, we show that a small subset of attention heads in the vision-language model OpenFlamingo-4B is responsible for transmitting representations of spatial relations. The activations of these attention heads, termed function vectors, can be extracted and manipulated to alter an LMM's performance on relational tasks. First, using both synthetic and real image datasets, we apply causal mediation analysis to identify attention heads that strongly influence relational predictions, and extract multimodal function vectors that improve zero-shot accuracy at inference time. We further demonstrate that these multimodal function vectors can be fine-tuned with a modest amount of training data, while keeping LMM parameters frozen, to significantly outperform in-context learning baselines. Finally, we show that relation-specific function vectors can be linearly combined to solve analogy problems involving novel and untrained spatial relations, highlighting the strong generalization ability of this approach. Our results show that LMMs encode spatial relational knowledge within localized internal structures, which can be systematically extracted and optimized, thereby advancing our understanding of model modularity and enhancing control over relational reasoning in LMMs.

papers.title: Investigating Representation Universality: Case Study on Genealogical Representations
papers.research_question: Do LLMs exhibit representation universality when encoding graph-structured knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that LLMs may employ universal geometric structures to encode graph-structured knowledge, through identification of a tree-like subspace via a cone probe and model stitching experiments showing representational alignment across models.
papers.conclusion: The lack of ground truth representations of graphs makes it challenging to study how LLMs represent them, but improving understanding of LLM representations could facilitate more interpretable, robust, and controllable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs represent genealogical relationships in a tree-like geometric structure (cone embedding) that can be isolated via a cone probe.
Activation patching shows that the cone subspace is causally relevant for answering descendant-of questions.
Model stitching experiments show that representations align more in early to mid layers than later layers, supporting representation universality.
The cone probe yields clearer tree structure than PCA projections.
Models struggle with compositional generalization when graph descriptions are shuffled (reversal curse).
papers.limitation:
Focus solely on internal geometry and universality without examining how subspaces are leveraged by the model for answering questions (circuit analysis).
Experiments use a relatively small binary tree (15 nodes), so it remains unclear if similar causal, tree-like subspaces emerge in larger or more complex genealogies.
Model stitching assumes representational alignment can be captured through a simple linear mapping, which may not hold for nonlinear representations.
Experiments span only a limited set of LLM architectures and scales, and may not generalize to other models like multimodal models.
future_direction: Systematically investigate optimal representations of more complex genealogical relationships (e.g., cousins, aunts, uncles).
Explore whether there exists a critical graph size beyond which optimal representations begin to emerge.
Examine how LLMs estimate their uncertainty when reasoning over graph-structured data.
papers.abstract: Motivated by interpretability and reliability, we investigate whether large language models (LLMs) deploy universal geometric structures to encode discrete, graph-structured knowledge. To this end, we present two complementary experimental evidence that might support universality of graph representations. First, on an in-context genealogy Q&A task, we train a cone probe to isolate a tree-like subspace in residual stream activations and use activation patching to verify its causal effect in answering related questions. We validate our findings across five different models. Second, we conduct model stitching experiments across models of diverse architectures and parameter counts (OPT, Pythia, Mistral, and LLaMA, 410 million to 8 billion parameters), quantifying representational alignment via relative degradation in the next-token prediction loss. Generally, we conclude that the lack of ground truth representations of graphs makes it challenging to study how LLMs represent them. Ultimately, improving our understanding of LLM representations could facilitate the development of more interpretable, robust, and controllable AI systems.

papers.title: Relational Composition in Neural Networks: A Survey and Call to Action
papers.research_question: How do neural networks represent relational composition of features, and what are the implications for interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: This paper surveys existing mechanisms for relational composition in neural networks and argues that understanding these mechanisms is crucial for interpretability, highlighting potential issues like feature multiplicity and dark matter.
papers.conclusion: The paper advocates for continued research into relational composition mechanisms, as identifying them would advance interpretability, and even their absence would be an important theoretical result.
papers.key_findings:
Feature multiplicity may occur, where multiple distinct vectors correspond to the same concept, complicating interpretability.
Dark matter may exist, where some features or combinations are systematically hidden from standard feature identification methods.
Predict/control discrepancy may arise, where vectors for predicting network behavior differ from those for controlling it.
Relational composition mechanisms (e.g., additive matrix binding, multi-token mechanisms, vector symbolic architectures) could be present in neural networks and affect interpretability.
Understanding relational composition is essential for advancing interpretability and could help organize feature catalogs.
papers.limitation: The arguments are conjectural and often involve idealized settings.
future_direction: Toy models that learn composition.
Apply feature extraction methods to synthetic composition mechanisms.
Apply dictionary learning to token differences.
papers.abstract: Many neural nets appear to represent data as linear combinations of "feature vectors." Algorithms for discovering these vectors have seen impressive recent success. However, we argue that this success is incomplete without an understanding of relational composition: how (or whether) neural nets combine feature vectors to represent more complicated relationships. To facilitate research in this area, this paper offers a guided tour of various relational mechanisms that have been proposed, along with preliminary analysis of how such mechanisms might affect the search for interpretable features. We end with a series of promising areas for empirical research, which may help determine how neural networks represent structured data.

papers.title: The Shape of Beliefs: Geometry, Dynamics, and Interventions along Representation Manifolds of Language Models' Posteriors
papers.research_question: How are prompt-conditioned beliefs encoded in representation space, how do they update with new evidence, and how can interventions reshape them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that beliefs in LLMs are encoded as curved manifolds in representation space, and that linear steering often fails to preserve the intended belief family, while geometry-aware steering based on linear field probes is more effective.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction, highlighting the importance of geometry-aware methods for interpretability and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Belief manifolds for distribution parameters (mean and standard deviation) are curved in representation space.
Linear field probes can tile the manifold and decode parameters with high accuracy and smooth variation.
When the input distribution changes, the model updates its beliefs along trajectories on the manifold, with different timescales for mean and variance.
Linear steering can push activations off-manifold, causing coupled shifts in other parameters (e.g., variance).
Geometry-aware steering using linear field probes better preserves the intended belief family and avoids unintended coupled shifts.
papers.limitation:
Relies on small open-source base models and focuses on a restricted family of prompt distributions (time-series), which may not capture the diversity of internal geometries in other settings.
The assumption that beliefs live on manifolds indexable by interpretable parameters may not hold in natural language tasks where latent variables are not fully parameterizable.
Does not investigate causal attribution to uncover which neuronal structure or circuits are responsible for the observed geometry.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) represent prompt-conditioned beliefs (posteriors over answers and claims), but we lack a mechanistic account of how these beliefs are encoded in representation space, how they update with new evidence, and how interventions reshape them. We study a controlled setting in which Llama-3.2 generates samples from a normal distribution by implicitly inferring its parameters (mean and standard deviation) given only samples from the distribution in context. We find representations of curved "belief manifolds" for these parameters form with sufficient in-context learning and study how the model adapts when the distribution suddenly changes. While standard linear steering often pushes the model off-manifold and induces coupled, out-of-distribution shifts, geometry and field-aware steering better preserves the intended belief family. Our work demonstrates an example of linear field probing (LFP) as a simple approach to tile the data manifold and make interventions that respect the underlying geometry. We conclude that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction.

papers.title: Linear Spatial World Models Emerge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly encode linear spatial world models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides empirical evidence that large language models encode linear spatial world models, showing that spatial relations are represented in a low-dimensional subspace with geometric structure and are functionally used by the model.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that large language models do encode a basic spatial world model linearly within their representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes achieve near-perfect accuracy in decoding spatial relations, indicating linear encoding.
PCA reveals a low-dimensional subspace where spatial relations are organized geometrically (inverse relations are antipodal, orthogonal relations are perpendicular).
Spatial representations are compositional: composed relations correspond to vector sums of atomic relations.
Object positions are consistently represented in the same spatial subspace.
Causal interventions (activation steering) show that the spatial subspace is functionally used by the model for prediction.
papers.limitation:
The work does not investigate other essential components of a full world model, such as temporal dynamics or object permanence.
The analysis focuses on a limited set of spatial relations.
The generality of the findings to other model types remains an open question.
future_direction: Extending the framework to cover a broader and more diverse set of spatial directions.
Investigating other components of world models such as temporal dynamics.
Testing generalization to other model types.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated emergent abilities across diverse tasks, raising the question of whether they acquire internal world models. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs implicitly encode linear spatial world models, which we define as linear representations of physical space and object configurations. We introduce a formal framework for spatial world models and assess whether such structure emerges in contextual embeddings. Using a synthetic dataset of object positions, we train probes to decode object positions and evaluate geometric consistency of the underlying space. We further conduct causal interventions to test whether these spatial representations are functionally used by the model. Our results provide empirical evidence that LLMs encode linear spatial world models.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: Probing Linguistic Features of Sentence-Level Representations in Neural Relation Extraction
papers.research_question: What linguistic features do neural relation extraction models learn in their sentence representations, and how do encoder architectures and input features affect these learned features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces 14 probing tasks for relation extraction and uses them to analyze how encoder architectures and linguistic features affect the learned sentence representations, finding clear architectural biases and feature effects.
papers.conclusion: Probing tasks reveal how architectural biases and input features affect learned representations, with self-attentive encoders capturing deeper features not captured by the probing tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Adding contextualized word representations (ELMo, BERT) increases performance on probing tasks focusing on named entity and part-of-speech information and improves RE performance.
Entity masking improves RE performance but considerably lowers performance on entity type related probing tasks.
Self-attentive encoders perform well on RE but consistently perform lower on the probing tasks, suggesting they capture 'deeper' linguistic features not covered by the current probing tasks.
The bias induced by different encoder architectures clearly affects the learned properties, e.g., local models (CNN, BiLSTM) perform well on local probing tasks, while GCN performs well on dependency-related tasks.
Probing task performance does not necessarily correlate with downstream RE task performance.
papers.limitation: The probing tasks do not cover all linguistic patterns, such as appositions, and do not investigate generalization to specific entity types.
future_direction: Extend the probing tasks to cover specific linguistic patterns such as appositions.
Investigate a model's ability of generalizing to specific entity types, e.g., company and person names.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent progress, little is known about the features captured by state-of-the-art neural relation extraction (RE) models. Common methods encode the source sentence, conditioned on the entity mentions, before classifying the relation. However, the complexity of the task makes it difficult to understand how encoder architecture and supporting linguistic knowledge affect the features learned by the encoder. We introduce 14 probing tasks targeting linguistic properties relevant to RE, and we use them to study representations learned by more than 40 different encoder architecture and linguistic feature combinations trained on two datasets, TACRED and SemEval 2010 Task 8. We find that the bias induced by the architecture and the inclusion of linguistic features are clearly expressed in the probing task performance. For example, adding contextualized word representations greatly increases performance on probing tasks with a focus on named entity and part-of-speech information, and yields better results in RE. In contrast, entity masking improves RE, but considerably lowers performance on entity type related probing tasks.

papers.title: Out-of-Context Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How well can large language models reason about binary relations (equality, inequality, inclusion) when the axioms are only seen during training and not provided in the task prompt?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces out-of-context representation learning, a lightweight technique that trains only new token embeddings, and shows it enables LLMs to reason about binary relations better than in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Out-of-context representation learning allows for better generalization in reasoning about binary relations, and models succeed by arranging learned embeddings according to the task.
papers.key_findings:
Out-of-context representation learning performs better than in-context learning for most binary relation tasks.
Models succeed in illustrative settings (with diverse and balanced data) but struggle with minimal settings.
Learned embeddings are structured (e.g., for total order, they resemble number embeddings arranged on an axis).
The reversal curse may stem from linguistic ambiguity and can be overcome with proper training.
A distance effect is observed: accuracy increases with the distance between symbols in the relation.
papers.limitation:
The learned representations are noisy and subject to errors for short-distance comparisons.
The study does not employ Chain of Thought, which could be a limitation for reasoning analysis.
future_direction: Test the robustness of out-of-context representation learning against data contamination by repeating experiments on models trained on plain text versions of the experiments.
Check whether a model can generate chains of thought while not being explicitly trained to do so.
papers.abstract: We study how large language models (LLMs) reason about memorized knowledge through simple binary relations such as equality ($=$), inequality ($<$), and inclusion ($\subset$). Unlike in-context reasoning, the axioms (e.g., $a < b, b < c$) are only seen during training and not provided in the task prompt (e.g., evaluating $a < c$). The tasks require one or more reasoning steps, and data aggregation from one or more sources, showing performance change with task complexity. We introduce a lightweight technique, out-of-context representation learning, which trains only new token embeddings on axioms and evaluates them on unseen tasks. Across reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity tests, LLMs mostly perform statistically significant better than chance, making the correct answer extractable when testing multiple phrasing variations, but still fall short of consistent reasoning on every single query. Analysis shows that the learned embeddings are organized in structured ways, suggesting real relational understanding. Surprisingly, it also indicates that the core reasoning happens during the training, not inference.

papers.title: Demystifying Relational Latent Representations
papers.research_question: What do latent features mean, and what makes latent representations effective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that relational latent features created by clustering are interpretable, capture sensible data properties, identify local regions that align with labels, and are often redundant, allowing for removal without significant performance loss.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that relational latent features are interpretable, capture local label-aligned regions, and are redundant, allowing for simplification without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Latent features are interpretable and capture interesting properties of data.
Latent features identify local regions of instances that match well with the label, which partially explains their benefit.
Latent representations have lower label entropy and higher sparsity compared to original representations, making learning easier.
Many latent features are redundant and can be removed without hurting performance much.
The method for extracting meaning using θ-confidence provides transparent explanations of latent features.
papers.limitation: The explanation of latent features does not conform to the standard first-order logic syntax common within relational learning.
papers.abstract: Latent features learned by deep learning approaches have proven to be a powerful tool for machine learning. They serve as a data abstraction that makes learning easier by capturing regularities in data explicitly. Their benefits motivated their adaptation to relational learning context. In our previous work, we introduce an approach that learns relational latent features by means of clustering instances and their relations. The major drawback of latent representations is that they are often black-box and difficult to interpret. This work addresses these issues and shows that (1) latent features created by clustering are interpretable and capture interesting properties of data; (2) they identify local regions of instances that match well with the label, which partially explains their benefit; and (3) although the number of latent features generated by this approach is large, often many of them are highly redundant and can be removed without hurting performance much.

papers.title: Finding patterns in Knowledge Attribution for Transformers
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how factual, relational, and grammatical knowledge are attributed to neurons in different layers of a transformer model, and whether multilingual facts share the same neurons.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that factual knowledge is attributed to middle and higher layers, relational knowledge to middle layers, and grammatical knowledge is more dispersed. It also shows that multilingual facts share neurons, indicating a common representation space.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents patterns on the location of different types of knowledge in transformer networks and their interactions across languages using the Knowledge Neurons attribution technique.
papers.key_findings:
Factual knowledge is attributed to middle and higher layers (>=6).
Relational knowledge is mostly in layers 6-9, and factual knowledge is refined in layers 10-12.
The same neurons are activated for facts in different languages, indicating a common representation space.
Grammatical knowledge is more dispersed across layers compared to factual knowledge.
The number of attractors in grammatical tasks affects attribution scores and variation.
future_direction: Explore other attribution techniques
Apply analysis to other language models like GPT
papers.abstract: We analyze the Knowledge Neurons framework for the attribution of factual and relational knowledge to particular neurons in the transformer network. We use a 12-layer multi-lingual BERT model for our experiments. Our study reveals various interesting phenomena. We observe that mostly factual knowledge can be attributed to middle and higher layers of the network($\ge 6$). Further analysis reveals that the middle layers($6-9$) are mostly responsible for relational information, which is further refined into actual factual knowledge or the "correct answer" in the last few layers($10-12$). Our experiments also show that the model handles prompts in different languages, but representing the same fact, similarly, providing further evidence for effectiveness of multi-lingual pre-training. Applying the attribution scheme for grammatical knowledge, we find that grammatical knowledge is far more dispersed among the neurons than factual knowledge.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Acquire New Knowledge? A Knowledge Circuits Perspective on Continual Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) structurally embed and acquire new knowledge during continual pre-training, from the perspective of knowledge circuit evolution?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the evolution of knowledge circuits during continual pre-training, revealing that new knowledge acquisition is influenced by relevance to existing knowledge, follows a biphasic (formation then optimization) pattern, and exhibits a deep-to-shallow component evolution.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the theoretical understanding of new knowledge acquisition mechanisms in LLMs and provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The acquisition of new knowledge is significantly influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge, with relevant new knowledge being integrated more efficiently than completely new knowledge.
The evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization, each marked by unique structural and behavioral characteristics.
The evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern, where mid-to-deeper layers first develop the extraction function, and later, lower layers enrich their knowledge representations.
The performance of knowledge circuits is positively correlated with knowledge frequency, with low-frequency knowledge circuits suffering from insufficient representations rather than fundamental capacity limitations.
The state of knowledge circuits could serve as a valuable tracking status for the continual pre-training process, enabling more informed adjustments to training.
future_direction: Utilizing data curriculums in continual pre-training to mimic the structure of the original corpus for more efficient integration.
Using the state of knowledge circuits as a tracking status to enable informed adjustments to training methods or data in response to different phases.
Further investigation into knowledge capacity scaling laws and their impact on model behavior during continual pre-training.
papers.abstract: Despite exceptional capabilities in knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) face a critical gap in understanding how they internalize new knowledge, particularly how to structurally embed acquired knowledge in their neural computations. We address this issue through the lens of knowledge circuit evolution, identifying computational subgraphs that facilitate knowledge storage and processing. Our systematic analysis of circuit evolution throughout continual pre-training reveals several key findings: (1) the acquisition of new knowledge is influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge; (2) the evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization; (3) the evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern. These insights not only advance our theoretical understanding of the mechanisms of new knowledge acquisition in LLMs, but also provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/zjunlp/DynamicKnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Toward a Flexible Framework for Linear Representation Hypothesis Using Maximum Likelihood Estimation
papers.research_question: How can we generalize the linear representation hypothesis to handle complex, context-dependent concepts without relying on single-token counterfactual pairs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generalized framework that redefines binary concepts as unit vectors in a canonical representation space and uses activation differences formalized via a von Mises-Fisher distribution and maximum likelihood estimation to compute concept directions, eliminating the need for single-token counterfactual pairs.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a generalized framework that bridges linear representation hypothesis and representation engineering, offering a principled and robust method for constructing concept directions that is lightweight, flexible, and effective for monitoring and manipulating LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed SAND method consistently outperforms PCA and zero-shot baselines in monitoring truthfulness and other QA tasks across LLaMA models.
SAND accurately captures concept directions (e.g., for gender, case, language) for steering interventions, whereas PCA fails in some cases.
SAND is computationally efficient, requiring only one matrix multiplication, making it lightweight and easy to integrate into existing activation engineering pipelines.
The method provides theoretical justification for the empirical effectiveness of the heuristic Mean Difference method for extracting steering vectors.
The framework bridges the gap between the theory of linear representation hypothesis and the practice of representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Linear representation hypothesis posits that high-level concepts are encoded as linear directions in the representation spaces of LLMs. Park et al. (2024) formalize this notion by unifying multiple interpretations of linear representation, such as 1-dimensional subspace representation and interventions, using a causal inner product. However, their framework relies on single-token counterfactual pairs and cannot handle ambiguous contrasting pairs, limiting its applicability to complex or context-dependent concepts. We introduce a new notion of binary concepts as unit vectors in a canonical representation space, and utilize LLMs' (neural) activation differences along with maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to compute concept directions (i.e., steering vectors). Our method, Sum of Activation-base Normalized Difference (SAND), formalizes the use of activation differences modeled as samples from a von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distribution, providing a principled approach to derive concept directions. We extend the applicability of Park et al. (2024) by eliminating the dependency on unembedding representations and single-token pairs. Through experiments with LLaMA models across diverse concepts and benchmarks, we demonstrate that our lightweight approach offers greater flexibility, superior performance in activation engineering tasks like monitoring and manipulation.

papers.title: Emergence of Linear Truth Encodings in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why and how do linear truth subspaces that separate true from false statements emerge in language models during training and inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the statistical co-occurrence of true/false statements (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis), demonstrated through a toy transformer model and experiments.
papers.conclusion: Linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the co-occurrence statistics of true and false statements, as demonstrated by a toy model and supported by experiments in pretrained models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear truth encoding emerges in a one-layer transformer trained on data where true/false statements co-occur (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis).
Training exhibits two phases: fast memorization of factual associations followed by slower development of linear truth separation.
Layer normalization is necessary for the linear separability of true and false representations.
The value matrix develops a block structure that enables sharpening of predictions for true sequences.
Experiments with Pythia-6.9B show similar two-phase dynamics in a large pretrained model.
papers.limitation:
The toy model is far simpler than natural training data, so the mechanism might not fully capture real-world complexity.
In real LMs, additional mechanisms likely contribute to truth encoding.
future_direction: Systematic study of mechanisms for truth encoding in real LMs.
Generalization of truth encoding across different relations.
papers.abstract: Recent probing studies reveal that large language models exhibit linear subspaces that separate true from false statements, yet the mechanism behind their emergence is unclear. We introduce a transparent, one-layer transformer toy model that reproduces such truth subspaces end-to-end and exposes one concrete route by which they can arise. We study one simple setting in which truth encoding can emerge: a data distribution where factual statements co-occur with other factual statements (and vice-versa), encouraging the model to learn this distinction in order to lower the LM loss on future tokens.
