papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: What Has Been Enhanced in my Knowledge-Enhanced Language Model?
papers.research_question: What knowledge is effectively integrated into knowledge-enhanced language models, and does integration lead to catastrophic forgetting of existing knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Graph Convolution Simulator (GCS), an information-theoretic probe for interpreting knowledge integration in language models, and finds that only a marginal amount of knowledge is successfully integrated and that increasing corpus size does not guarantee better integration.
papers.conclusion: Derived an information-theoretic probe (GCS) that uses attention over knowledge graphs to interpret knowledge integration, verified it experimentally, and used it to gain new insights into two knowledge-enhanced language models.
papers.key_findings:
GCS provides reasonable interpretation results for ERNIE and K-Adapter with lower variance than linear probes.
Only a marginal amount of knowledge (less than 30% of triples) is successfully integrated in ERNIE and K-Adapter.
ERNIE integrates triples with high-degree entities better, while K-Adapter integrates triples with low-degree entities well.
Enhanced LMs do not integrate numerical and temporal knowledge well.
There is no positive relationship between knowledge integration corpus size and integration quality.
papers.limitation:
Simplifies the knowledge graph without considering relation information such as labels.
GCS only interprets knowledge integration; improving integration quality remains challenging.
future_direction: Handling relation information in knowledge graphs.
Improving knowledge integration quality.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (LMs) do not capture factual knowledge very well. This has led to the development of a number of knowledge integration (KI) methods which aim to incorporate external knowledge into pretrained LMs. Even though KI methods show some performance gains over vanilla LMs, the inner-workings of these methods are not well-understood. For instance, it is unclear how and what kind of knowledge is effectively integrated into these models and if such integration may lead to catastrophic forgetting of already learned knowledge. This paper revisits the KI process in these models with an information-theoretic view and shows that KI can be interpreted using a graph convolution operation. We propose a probe model called \textit{Graph Convolution Simulator} (GCS) for interpreting knowledge-enhanced LMs and exposing what kind of knowledge is integrated into these models. We conduct experiments to verify that our GCS can indeed be used to correctly interpret the KI process, and we use it to analyze two well-known knowledge-enhanced LMs: ERNIE and K-Adapter, and find that only a small amount of factual knowledge is integrated in them. We stratify knowledge in terms of various relation types and find that ERNIE and K-Adapter integrate different kinds of knowledge to different extent. Our analysis also shows that simply increasing the size of the KI corpus may not lead to better KI; fundamental advances may be needed.

papers.title: Attention Mechanisms Perspective: Exploring LLM Processing of Graph-Structured Data
papers.research_question: How do LLMs process graph-structured data from the perspective of attention mechanisms, and do they effectively utilize graph connectivity information?
papers.core_contribution: This paper empirically studies LLM attention on graph-structured data, finding that LLMs struggle to model inter-node relationships due to architectural constraints, and that intermediate attention windows (neither fully connected nor fixed-link) improve training and inference performance.
papers.conclusion: The work explores LLM attention mechanisms on graph data, discovers multiple phenomena, and provides directional guidance for future research in graph machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can recognize graph data and capture text-node interactions but struggle to model inter-node relationships within graph structures.
The attention distribution of LLMs across graph nodes does not align with ideal structural patterns, indicating a failure to adapt to graph topology nuances.
Neither fully connected attention nor fixed connectivity is optimal; intermediate-state attention windows improve LLM training performance and transfer well to fully connected windows during inference.
The study identifies 'Attention Sink' issues similar to NLP tasks and a unique 'Skewed Line Sink' phenomenon specific to graph data.
Training LLMs with a smaller linkage horizon (incorporating some topological information) and then transferring to a larger horizon during inference enhances performance and addresses deployment challenges.
papers.limitation: Due to limitations in length and resources, only a portion of the discovered phenomena were analyzed; many unexplored phenomena remain.
future_direction: Explore methods to correct attention biases (e.g., Attention Sink and Skewed Line Sink) to improve model performance.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms are critical to the success of large language models (LLMs), driving significant advancements in multiple fields. However, for graph-structured data, which requires emphasis on topological connections, they fall short compared to message-passing mechanisms on fixed links, such as those employed by Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). This raises a question: ``Does attention fail for graphs in natural language settings?'' Motivated by these observations, we embarked on an empirical study from the perspective of attention mechanisms to explore how LLMs process graph-structured data. The goal is to gain deeper insights into the attention behavior of LLMs over graph structures. We uncovered unique phenomena regarding how LLMs apply attention to graph-structured data and analyzed these findings to improve the modeling of such data by LLMs. The primary findings of our research are: 1) While LLMs can recognize graph data and capture text-node interactions, they struggle to model inter-node relationships within graph structures due to inherent architectural constraints. 2) The attention distribution of LLMs across graph nodes does not align with ideal structural patterns, indicating a failure to adapt to graph topology nuances. 3) Neither fully connected attention nor fixed connectivity is optimal; each has specific limitations in its application scenarios. Instead, intermediate-state attention windows improve LLM training performance and seamlessly transition to fully connected windows during inference. Source code: \href{https://github.com/millioniron/LLM_exploration}{LLM4Exploration}

papers.title: Tracing the complexity profiles of different linguistic phenomena through the intrinsic dimension of LLM representations
papers.research_question: Does the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations serve as a marker for linguistic complexity, and can it differentiate between formal and functional complexity?
papers.core_contribution: The intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations is a useful marker for linguistic complexity, allowing differentiation between formal and functional complexity, and points to similar stages of linguistic processing across disparate LLMs.
papers.conclusion: ID is a useful marker of linguistic complexity in LLMs, it allows differentiation between formal and functional complexity, and it points to similar stages of linguistic processing across disparate LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
ID profiles differentiate between formal complexity (coordination vs. subordination) and functional complexity (right-branching vs. center-embedding, unambiguous vs. ambiguous).
The formal complexity contrast emerges in layers coinciding with the generic ID peak, a phase of deep linguistic processing.
Functional complexity contrasts are also reflected in ID but in a less marked way and not correlated with the same processing phase.
Representational similarity (Information Imbalance) and ablation experiments confirm these trends.
Different LLMs show consistent ID profiles and processing stages.
papers.limitation:
Due to compute restrictions, experiments cannot be extended to larger language models.
Results should be reproduced in languages other than English and with more naturalistic data.
A clear mechanistic explanation of the relation between intrinsic dimension and the linguistic phenomena is needed.
future_direction: Ascertain the extent to which observed patterns depend on model size and their emergence during training.
Reproduce results in languages other than English and with more naturalistic data.
Establish a clear mechanistic explanation of the relation between intrinsic dimension and linguistic phenomena.
papers.abstract: We explore the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations as a marker of linguistic complexity, asking if different ID profiles across LLM layers differentially characterize formal and functional complexity. We find the formal contrast between sentences with multiple coordinated or subordinated clauses to be reflected in ID differences whose onset aligns with a phase of more abstract linguistic processing independently identified in earlier work. The functional contrasts between sentences characterized by right branching vs. center embedding or unambiguous vs. ambiguous relative clause attachment are also picked up by ID, but in a less marked way, and they do not correlate with the same processing phase. Further experiments using representational similarity and layer ablation confirm the same trends. We conclude that ID is a useful marker of linguistic complexity in LLMs, that it allows to differentiate between different types of complexity, and that it points to similar stages of linguistic processing across disparate LLMs.

papers.title: On Linear Representations and Pretraining Data Frequency in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the connection between pretraining data frequency and the formation of linear representations of factual relations in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The formation of linear representations for factual recall in language models is strongly correlated with pretraining term frequencies, and measuring these representations allows prediction of term frequencies in the pretraining corpus.
papers.conclusion: Linear representations of factual triplets in LMs are connected to pretraining frequencies, which can guide interpretability work and enable prediction of term frequencies in closed-data models.
papers.key_findings:
The development of linear representations for factual recall relations in LMs is related to frequency as well as model size.
Linear representations form at predictable frequency thresholds during training, regardless of when this threshold is met, and correlate strongly with recall accuracy.
Measuring the extent to which a relation is represented linearly allows prediction of the approximate frequencies of individual terms in the pretraining corpus, even without access to the training data.
The predictive signal from linear representations is stronger than that from log probabilities and task accuracies alone.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on factual relations and leaves non-factual relations (e.g., gender stereotypes) for future work.
The regression model provides approximate frequency predictions within bounds, not exact counts.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to non-factual relations.
Improve the bounds of predicted frequencies.
Understand if and when LMs use non-linear methods to solve tasks.
papers.abstract: Pretraining data has a direct impact on the behaviors and quality of language models (LMs), but we only understand the most basic principles of this relationship. While most work focuses on pretraining data's effect on downstream task behavior, we investigate its relationship to LM representations. Previous work has discovered that, in language models, some concepts are encoded `linearly' in the representations, but what factors cause these representations to form? We study the connection between pretraining data frequency and models' linear representations of factual relations. We find evidence that the formation of linear representations is strongly connected to pretraining term frequencies; specifically for subject-relation-object fact triplets, both subject-object co-occurrence frequency and in-context learning accuracy for the relation are highly correlated with linear representations. This is the case across all phases of pretraining. In OLMo-7B and GPT-J, we discover that a linear representation consistently (but not exclusively) forms when the subjects and objects within a relation co-occur at least 1k and 2k times, respectively, regardless of when these occurrences happen during pretraining. Finally, we train a regression model on measurements of linear representation quality in fully-trained LMs that can predict how often a term was seen in pretraining. Our model achieves low error even on inputs from a different model with a different pretraining dataset, providing a new method for estimating properties of the otherwise-unknown training data of closed-data models. We conclude that the strength of linear representations in LMs contains signal about the models' pretraining corpora that may provide new avenues for controlling and improving model behavior: particularly, manipulating the models' training data to meet specific frequency thresholds.

papers.title: From Directions to Cones: Exploring Multidimensional Representations of Propositional Facts in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does truth in LLMs have a multi-dimensional representation (concept cone) rather than a single linear direction, and can such cones causally mediate truth-related behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that truth in LLMs is represented as a multi-dimensional cone in activation space, and that interventions using these cones can reliably steer model outputs on true/false propositions while preserving unrelated capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Multi-dimensional concept cones can reliably steer LLM behavior on true/false propositions across architectures and sizes, revealing a robust subspace of activation vectors that modulate factuality.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-related directions are localized in middle to later layers, with the final token position being most effective for interventions.
Multi-dimensional concept cones for truth exist and can causally mediate truthful behavior across different model families and sizes.
Increasing cone dimensionality generally improves steering effectiveness, but beyond a point, ASR declines, especially in smaller models.
The discovered truth directions are specific and do not significantly affect general instruction-following capabilities (low KL divergence on Alpaca).
The classic DIM direction aligns only with the first axis of the cone; other axes are orthogonal, indicating additional structure.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on relatively small open-source models (1.5B–7B parameters) and may not generalize to larger frontier models.
The operationalization of truth is narrow, limited to simple unambiguous propositional facts, and does not capture more complex notions of truth.
The method does not guarantee discovery of a maximally informative or interpretable subspace, and individual cone axes lack semantic meaning.
future_direction: Pair cones with automated clustering or sparse autoencoding to assign semantic meaning to basis vectors.
Extend the method to larger, instruction-tuned models.
Extend to multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong conversational abilities but often generate falsehoods. Prior work suggests that the truthfulness of simple propositions can be represented as a single linear direction in a model's internal activations, but this may not fully capture its underlying geometry. In this work, we extend the concept cone framework, recently introduced for modeling refusal, to the domain of truth. We identify multi-dimensional cones that causally mediate truth-related behavior across multiple LLM families. Our results are supported by three lines of evidence: (i) causal interventions reliably flip model responses to factual statements, (ii) learned cones generalize across model architectures, and (iii) cone-based interventions preserve unrelated model behavior. These findings reveal the richer, multidirectional structure governing simple true/false propositions in LLMs and highlight concept cones as a promising tool for probing abstract behaviors.

papers.title: Low-Dimensional Structure in the Space of Language Representations is Reflected in Brain Responses
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks? Does the low-dimensional structure of these representations correspond to brain responses during language processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a low-dimensional structure in the space of language representations and shows that this structure can predict how well each representation maps to human brain responses to natural language, suggesting it captures part of the brain's natural language representation hierarchy.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure in language representations reflects the brain's natural language processing hierarchy, suggesting that the embedding captures some part of the brain's representation structure.
papers.key_findings:
A low-dimensional structure exists in the space of language representations, with the first MDS dimension capturing a progression from word embeddings to syntactic/semantic tasks to next-word embeddings.
The representation embeddings can predict fMRI encoding model performance, indicating a link between the representation space and brain responses.
Projecting the first MDS dimension onto the brain recovers known language processing hierarchies, with early auditory cortex explained by lower-level features and higher-order areas by later layers.
Most pairs of representations can be correctly matched to their brain response patterns using the representation embeddings.
The low-dimensional structure is consistent across different language models and translation models.
papers.limitation: Negative discriminability scores for some representation pairs, possibly due to disconnect between task affinities and brain representations, e.g., for GloVe next-word embedding.
papers.abstract: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks? We answer this question by adapting an encoder-decoder transfer learning method from computer vision to investigate the structure among 100 different feature spaces extracted from hidden representations of various networks trained on language tasks. This method reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models smoothly interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic and semantic tasks, and future word embeddings. We call this low-dimensional structure a language representation embedding because it encodes the relationships between representations needed to process language for a variety of NLP tasks. We find that this representation embedding can predict how well each individual feature space maps to human brain responses to natural language stimuli recorded using fMRI. Additionally, we find that the principal dimension of this structure can be used to create a metric which highlights the brain's natural language processing hierarchy. This suggests that the embedding captures some part of the brain's natural language representation structure.

papers.title: Decoding Knowledge in Large Language Models: A Framework for Categorization and Comprehension
papers.research_question: How can we categorize and analyze the knowledge in large language models by considering both correctness and confidence, and how do techniques like chain-of-thought prompting and instruction tuning affect this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the K-(CSA)² framework for categorizing LLM knowledge along dimensions of correctness and confidence, enabling a nuanced evaluation beyond binary accuracy and revealing how techniques like CoT and instruction tuning alter knowledge structures.
papers.conclusion: The K-(CSA)² framework provides systematic metrics for assessing LLMs' knowledge structures by evaluating correctness and confidence, revealing novel patterns in how knowledge is organized and evolves, which can benefit future model development.
papers.key_findings:
Stronger models are more assertive regardless of correctness, showing higher confidence in both correct and incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting creates synergistic benefits when combined with instruction tuning, improving both accuracy and category scores.
Instruction-tuned models show superior context understanding for external knowledge, with IT+CoT providing complementary benefits.
Higher layers in LLMs encode more high-confidence knowledge, while low-confidence knowledge tends to emerge in middle-to-lower layers.
Rising accuracy during pre-training does not guarantee better knowledge structure, as category scores can initially decrease before improving.
papers.limitation:
Relies heavily on sampling to determine confidence levels, where the number of samples and temperature settings could affect categorization results.
The boundaries between categories, especially for 'Maybe Known' and 'Weakly Known', can sometimes be ambiguous.
Evaluating models through multiple sampling runs is computationally intensive, which may limit the framework's applicability in resource-constrained scenarios.
Evaluation primarily focuses on factual knowledge in question-answering contexts and may need adaptation for other types of knowledge or tasks.
For external knowledge evaluation, the framework doesn't fully capture how models integrate multiple pieces of context or handle conflicting information.
future_direction: Exploring sampling robustness and strengthening theoretical foundations for category boundaries.
Extending the framework to more complex scenarios beyond factual QA.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) acquire, retain, and apply knowledge remains an open challenge. This paper introduces a novel framework, K-(CSA)^2, which categorizes LLM knowledge along two dimensions: correctness and confidence. The framework defines six categories of knowledge, ranging from highly confident correctness to confidently held misconceptions, enabling a nuanced evaluation of model comprehension beyond binary accuracy. Using this framework, we demonstrate how techniques like chain-of-thought prompting and reinforcement learning with human feedback fundamentally alter the knowledge structures of internal (pre-trained) and external (context-dependent) knowledge in LLMs. CoT particularly enhances base model performance and shows synergistic benefits when applied to aligned LLMs. Moreover, our layer-wise analysis reveals that higher layers in LLMs encode more high-confidence knowledge, while low-confidence knowledge tends to emerge in middle-to-lower layers.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize knowledge during training, and extract it later to answer questions or perform logical reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling) in pretraining data is crucial for reliable knowledge extraction via instruction fine-tuning, and introduces linear probing techniques to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes with practical recommendations for LLM pretraining: data rewriting (augmentation) is important, and including instruction-like data in pretraining is beneficial.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training (pretraining on both biographies and QA data) enables knowledge extraction, but the model learns in an abnormal way (first from QA then correlates with BIO).
Without knowledge augmentation in pretraining, instruction fine-tuning fails to extract knowledge (0% accuracy).
Knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) during pretraining enables knowledge extraction after fine-tuning.
Linear probing shows that knowledge augmentation causes knowledge to be linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names, whereas without augmentation it is distributed across tokens.
Including celebrity data (with augmentation) in pretraining improves knowledge extraction for minority data (without augmentation).
future_direction: Studying logical reasoning and knowledge manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a vast amount of world knowledge, often extractable via question-answering (e.g., "What is Abraham Lincoln's birthday?"). However, do they answer such questions based on exposure to similar questions during training (i.e., cheating), or by genuinely learning to extract knowledge from sources like Wikipedia? In this paper, we investigate this issue using a controlled biography dataset. We find a strong correlation between the model's ability to extract knowledge and various diversity measures of the training data. $\textbf{Essentially}$, for knowledge to be reliably extracted, it must be sufficiently augmented (e.g., through paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) $\textit{during pretraining}$. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized but not extractable, leading to 0% accuracy, regardless of subsequent instruction fine-tuning. To understand why this occurs, we employ (nearly) linear probing to demonstrate a strong connection between the observed correlation and how the model internally encodes knowledge -- whether it is linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names or distributed across other token embeddings in the training text. This paper provides $\textbf{several key recommendations for LLM pretraining in the industry}$: (1) rewrite the pretraining data -- using small, auxiliary models -- to provide knowledge augmentation, and (2) incorporate more instruction-finetuning data into the pretraining stage before it becomes too late.

papers.title: Fresh in memory: Training-order recency is linearly encoded in language model activations
papers.research_question: Do language models linearly encode when information was learned during training? Specifically, is training-order recency encoded in model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Language models linearly encode training-order recency in their activations, and this encoding is robust, generalizable, and accessible to the model itself.
papers.conclusion: Models linearly encode training-order information in their activations, a finding with significant implications for how models might manage conflicting data and respond to knowledge modifications.
papers.key_findings:
Activation centroids for test data from six sequential fine-tuning stages lie on a straight line in a 2D subspace, ordered exactly by training recency.
Linear probes can distinguish entities from the earliest and latest training stages with >90% accuracy, generalizing to held-out entities.
The encoding tracks recency: re-exposing a dataset moves its centroid to the 'most recent' position, and additional training on a stage pushes its centroid further.
The model can be fine-tuned to explicitly report an unseen entity's training stage with ~80% accuracy.
The encoding is not explained by simple activation statistics (norms, moments), output confidence, or geometric properties like PCA directions.
papers.limitation:
The persistence of the training-order signal through mixed-data training complicates a straightforward interpretation that the axis solely tracks exposure recency.
The signal for individual training datapoints (as opposed to entities) is weaker (~60% accuracy) and vanishes after mixed training, suggesting a different mechanism.
future_direction: Exploring whether fine-tuning access can be used to extract information about the order of pretraining data.
Finding a more precise interpretation of the training-order signal that accounts for its persistence through mixed-data training.
papers.abstract: We show that language models' activations linearly encode when information was learned during training. Our setup involves creating a model with a known training order by sequentially fine-tuning Llama-3.2-1B on six disjoint but otherwise similar datasets about named entities. We find that the average activations of test samples corresponding to the six training datasets encode the training order: when projected into a 2D subspace, these centroids are arranged exactly in the order of training and lie on a straight line. Further, we show that linear probes can accurately (~90%) distinguish "early" vs. "late" entities, generalizing to entities unseen during the probes' own training. The model can also be fine-tuned to explicitly report an unseen entity's training stage (~80% accuracy). Interestingly, the training-order encoding does not seem attributable to simple differences in activation magnitudes, losses, or model confidence. Our paper demonstrates that models are capable of differentiating information by its acquisition time, and carries significant implications for how they might manage conflicting data and respond to knowledge modifications.

papers.title: On the data requirements of probing
papers.research_question: How to estimate the required number of data samples for probing experiments to distinguish two different probing configurations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a framework to estimate data requirements for probing experiments, using generalization bounds to determine minimum training set sizes and verifying that recommendations provide sufficient statistical power.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework to estimate data requirements for probing experiments, which helps ensure that experiments have sufficient data to be scientifically meaningful, and calls for further work on systematic methodology for probing.
papers.key_findings:
The theoretical generalization bounds agree with empirical probing results.
Larger datasets provide higher statistical power to distinguish probing configurations.
The framework's recommended data sizes yield statistical power above 0.8 in various comparison problems.
Some comparison problems collapse (e.g., comparing logistic regression vs MLP on certain tasks) and cannot be distinguished even with large datasets.
The framework helps identify when additional data is needed for reliable comparisons.
papers.limitation:
Cross-task comparison problems are not considered because McNemar's test requires pairwise data.
The stability of theoretical recommendations can be affected by the suboptimality of probing classifiers.
The framework currently only applies to classification-based probing methods.
future_direction: Generalizing the framework to unsupervised probing methods.
Addressing cross-task comparison problems with alternative power tests.
Completing a systematic methodology for evaluating probing datasets and methods.
papers.abstract: As large and powerful neural language models are developed, researchers have been increasingly interested in developing diagnostic tools to probe them. There are many papers with conclusions of the form "observation X is found in model Y ", using their own datasets with varying sizes. Larger probing datasets bring more reliability, but are also expensive to collect.

papers.title: Large Language Models Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs' internal states reflect truthfulness or merely the process of recalling parametric knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs' internal states encode the process of knowledge recall, not truthfulness, making hallucination detection challenging for associated hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: Hidden states encode whether models rely on their parametric knowledge rather than truthfulness, so detection methods succeed for unassociated hallucinations but struggle for associated hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Associated Hallucinations (AHs) and Factual Associations (FAs) share similar internal processes and representational geometries.
Existing hallucination detection methods struggle to distinguish AHs from FAs, performing near random guessing.
Unassociated Hallucinations (UHs) are more separable in representation space and can be reliably detected.
Refusal tuning is less effective for AHs due to representational overlap with FAs, while it works better for UHs.
Subject popularity in pre-training data correlates with the prevalence of AHs and FAs, but not with UHs.
papers.limitation:
Focus on factual knowledge, not long-form or open-ended generation tasks
Lack of analysis on prompt-based hallucination detection approaches
Applicability limited to open-source LLMs, not black-box or large reasoning models
future_direction: Future evaluations should report detection performance separately for Associated Hallucinations and Unassociated Hallucinations.
Integrate LLMs with external feedback mechanisms, such as fact-checking modules or retrieval-based verifiers.
Prioritize improving detection of Associated Hallucinations due to their higher risk in practical deployments.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) encode factuality signals in their internal representations, such as hidden states, attention weights, or token probabilities, implying that LLMs may "know what they don't know". However, LLMs can also produce factual errors by relying on shortcuts or spurious associations. These error are driven by the same training objective that encourage correct predictions, raising the question of whether internal computations can reliably distinguish between factual and hallucinated outputs. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic analysis of how LLMs internally process factual queries by comparing two types of hallucinations based on their reliance on subject information. We find that when hallucinations are associated with subject knowledge, LLMs employ the same internal recall process as for correct responses, leading to overlapping and indistinguishable hidden-state geometries. In contrast, hallucinations detached from subject knowledge produce distinct, clustered representations that make them detectable. These findings reveal a fundamental limitation: LLMs do not encode truthfulness in their internal states but only patterns of knowledge recall, demonstrating that "LLMs don't really know what they don't know".

papers.title: Knowledge Localization: Mission Not Accomplished? Enter Query Localization!
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption hold for all facts? If not, what is a more realistic assumption?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Query Localization (QL) assumption, which includes query-KN mapping and dynamic KN selection, and introduces a Consistency-Aware KN modification method that improves knowledge editing performance.
papers.conclusion: The Query Localization assumption provides a more realistic framework for understanding knowledge storage and expression in LLMs than the Knowledge Localization assumption, and is validated by improved editing performance.
papers.key_findings:
Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) that violates the Knowledge Localization assumption is widespread in LLMs.
For KI, knowledge neurons are associated with specific queries rather than the fact itself (query-KN mapping).
The attention module plays a key role in selecting appropriate knowledge neurons for expression (dynamic KN selection).
The proposed Consistency-Aware KN modification method, based on the QL assumption, improves knowledge editing performance over baseline methods.
papers.limitation:
The work primarily focuses on factual knowledge, and it remains unclear whether the QL assumption applies to other types of knowledge.
The distinction between Consistent Knowledge (KC) and Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) might be related to the pre-training process.
future_direction: Exploring how to reconcile the QL assumption with other current theories.
Further utilizing the QL assumption to improve model editing methods.
Integrating the attention module more effectively to develop enhanced methods for dynamically editing knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store extensive factual knowledge, but the mechanisms behind how they store and express this knowledge remain unclear. The Knowledge Neuron (KN) thesis is a prominent theory for explaining these mechanisms. This theory is based on the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption, which suggests that a fact can be localized to a few knowledge storage units, namely knowledge neurons. However, this assumption has two limitations: first, it may be too rigid regarding knowledge storage, and second, it neglects the role of the attention module in knowledge expression. In this paper, we first re-examine the KL assumption and demonstrate that its limitations do indeed exist. To address these, we then present two new findings, each targeting one of the limitations: one focusing on knowledge storage and the other on knowledge expression. We summarize these findings as \textbf{Query Localization} (QL) assumption and argue that the KL assumption can be viewed as a simplification of the QL assumption. Based on QL assumption, we further propose the Consistency-Aware KN modification method, which improves the performance of knowledge modification, further validating our new assumption. We conduct 39 sets of experiments, along with additional visualization experiments, to rigorously confirm our conclusions. Code is available at https://github.com/heng840/KnowledgeLocalization.

papers.title: Predicting Fine-Tuning Performance with Probing
papers.research_question: Can probing results be used to predict the fine-tuning performance of deep NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that probing results can predict fine-tuning performance with errors 40%-80% smaller than baselines, using as few as three probing configurations.
papers.conclusion: Probing can be used to predict fine-tuning performance and has potential to improve model development efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Probing results from as few as three configurations can predict fine-tuning performance with high accuracy.
The most informative probing tasks and layers vary across fine-tuning tasks.
Probing is computationally efficient compared to fine-tuning.
The choice of probing method (e.g., MLP-20, RandomForest-100) affects predictability.
Probing with 400 samples per class still provides predictability, though less than with 1200 samples.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation is limited to classification tasks and may not generalize to other tasks like translation.
The method requires selecting probing tasks and layers, which may not be straightforward.
future_direction: Extending the method to non-classification tasks such as translation.
Incorporating probing into model development pipelines.
papers.abstract: Large NLP models have recently shown impressive performance in language understanding tasks, typically evaluated by their fine-tuned performance. Alternatively, probing has received increasing attention as being a lightweight method for interpreting the intrinsic mechanisms of large NLP models. In probing, post-hoc classifiers are trained on “out-of-domain” datasets that diagnose specific abilities. While probing the language models has led to insightful findings, they appear disjointed from the development of models. This paper explores the utility of probing deep NLP models to extract a proxy signal widely used in model development – the fine-tuning performance. We find that it is possible to use the accuracies of only three probing tests to predict the fine-tuning performance with errors 40% - 80% smaller than baselines. We further discuss possible avenues where probing can empower the development of deep NLP models.

papers.title: Hierarchical Deconstruction of LLM Reasoning: A Graph-Based Framework for Analyzing Knowledge Utilization
papers.research_question: How do large language models use their knowledge for reasoning when solving complex real-world questions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a graph-based framework to deconstruct questions by knowledge depth, introduces the DEPTH QA dataset, and analyzes forward and backward reasoning discrepancies in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: This work enhances our understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests ways to improve their problem-solving abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Smaller models exhibit larger forward and backward discrepancies compared to larger models.
Forward discrepancy occurs more frequently but with lower intensity, while backward discrepancy is less common but with higher intensity.
Memorization analysis shows that questions with lower memorization scores have higher discrepancies.
Multi-turn interactions that guide models from simpler to complex questions improve performance across model sizes.
Distinct patterns of discrepancies are observed across model capacities and memorization possibilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the advances in large language models (LLMs), how they use their knowledge for reasoning is not yet well understood. In this study, we propose a method that deconstructs complex real-world questions into a graph, representing each question as a node with predecessors of background knowledge needed to solve the question. We develop the DepthQA dataset, deconstructing questions into three depths: (i) recalling conceptual knowledge, (ii) applying procedural knowledge, and (iii) analyzing strategic knowledge. Based on a hierarchical graph, we quantify forward discrepancy, a discrepancy in LLM performance on simpler sub-problems versus complex questions. We also measure backward discrepancy where LLMs answer complex questions but struggle with simpler ones. Our analysis shows that smaller models exhibit more discrepancies than larger models. Distinct patterns of discrepancies are observed across model capacity and possibility of training data memorization. Additionally, guiding models from simpler to complex questions through multi-turn interactions improves performance across model sizes, highlighting the importance of structured intermediate steps in knowledge reasoning. This work enhances our understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests ways to improve their problem-solving abilities.

papers.title: Exploring the Role of BERT Token Representations to Explain Sentence Probing Results
papers.research_question: What role do specific token representations play in BERT's ability to encode linguistic features and explain probing results?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes linguistic features in specific token representations, and gradient-based attribution can reveal these subspaces to explain probing performance.
papers.conclusion: BERT's token representations encode specific linguistic knowledge, and attribution methods provide insights into probing results, revealing distinct subspaces for different features.
papers.key_findings:
Sentence-ending tokens retain positional information in higher layers.
The ##s token encodes both noun number and verb tense information, and BERT separates these usages into distinct subspaces.
In bi-gram shift tasks, inverted tokens have higher attribution scores, and abnormalities are encoded in their representations.
In coordination inversion, coordinators like 'and' and 'but' play a key role, and their representations change significantly.
Attribution patterns are consistent even with less training data, indicating that knowledge is well-encoded in representations.
future_direction: Investigate how subspaces evolve during fine-tuning
Check if behaviors are affected by different training objectives
Use token-level analysis for model efficiency
papers.abstract: Several studies have been carried out on revealing linguistic features captured by BERT. This is usually achieved by training a diagnostic classifier on the representations obtained from different layers of BERT. The subsequent classification accuracy is then interpreted as the ability of the model in encoding the corresponding linguistic property. Despite providing insights, these studies have left out the potential role of token representations. In this paper, we provide a more in-depth analysis on the representation space of BERT in search for distinct and meaningful subspaces that can explain the reasons behind these probing results. Based on a set of probing tasks and with the help of attribution methods we show that BERT tends to encode meaningful knowledge in specific token representations (which are often ignored in standard classification setups), allowing the model to detect syntactic and semantic abnormalities, and to distinctively separate grammatical number and tense subspaces. 1

papers.title: Relational reasoning and inductive bias in transformers and large language models
papers.research_question: How do transformers perform transitive inference, and how do inductive biases differ between in-weights learning (IWL) and in-context learning (ICL) strategies?
papers.core_contribution: IWL naturally induces transitive inference with symbolic distance and terminal item effects, while ICL models develop induction circuits that fail to generalize; however, pre-training on linear regression enables transitive inference in ICL without induction circuits.
papers.conclusion: Both the training regime and the geometric structure of induced representations critically determine transformers' capacity for transitive inference.
papers.key_findings:
IWL models exhibit transitive inference and show symbolic distance and terminal item effects despite training only on adjacent pairs.
ICL models trained only on adjacent pairs fail to generalize and rely on induction circuits implementing match-and-copy strategies.
Pre-training transformers on in-context linear regression tasks enables transitive inference in ICL without forming induction circuits.
Linear geometric prompts improve transitive inference in large language models, while circular prompts impair performance, especially when models cannot rely on stored knowledge.
The advantage of linear over circular prompting increases with model size for incongruent item pairs.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic analyses (PCA, ablation studies, attention patterns) were restricted to small transformer architectures for interpretability; internal mechanisms in LLMs remain opaque.
The transitive inference task is a simple example of relational reasoning which might not capture all real-world scenarios.
Results are empirical rather than theoretical.
future_direction: Combine experiments with advanced mechanistic interpretability techniques for LLMs.
Use transitive inference as a benchmark for evaluating model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have demonstrated remarkable reasoning abilities, but the mechanisms underlying relational reasoning remain poorly understood. We investigate how transformers perform \textit{transitive inference}, a classic relational reasoning task which requires inference indirectly related items (e.g., if $A>B$ and $B>C$, then $A>C$), comparing in-weights learning (IWL) and in-context learning (ICL) strategies. We find that IWL naturally induces a generalization bias towards transitive inference despite training only on adjacent items, whereas ICL models develop induction circuits implementing match-and-copy strategies that fail to encode hierarchical relationships. However, when pre-trained on in-context linear regression tasks, transformers successfully exhibit in-context generalizable transitive inference, displaying both \textit{symbolic distance} and \textit{terminal item effects} characteristic of human and animal performance, without forming induction circuits. We extend these findings to large language models, demonstrating that prompting with linear geometric scaffolds improves transitive inference, while circular geometries (which violate transitivity by allowing wraparound) impair performance, particularly when models cannot rely on stored knowledge. Together, these results reveal that both the training regime and the geometric structure of induced representations critically determine transformers' capacity for transitive inference.

papers.title: Time Course MechInterp: Analyzing the Evolution of Components and Knowledge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do the components (attention heads and FFNs) responsible for factual knowledge in a large language model evolve during pre-training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that during pre-training, LLMs start with general-purpose components that later specialize, with attention heads showing high role turnover while FFNs remain stable.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a mechanistic view of how factual knowledge forms in LLMs, showing a dynamic specialization process for attention heads and stable FFNs.
papers.key_findings:
Location-based relations converge to high accuracy earlier in training than name-based relations.
Attention heads initially depend on general-purpose roles and later specialize as training progresses.
Attention heads exhibit high role turnover, especially answer-specific heads.
FFNs remain more stable throughout training, acting as a steady processing backbone.
Once the model reliably predicts answers, some components are repurposed, suggesting an adaptive learning process.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints prevented analysis at the neuron level, potentially missing finer-grained switching behaviors.
The dataset is limited to English and covers only location-based and name-based relations, limiting generalizability.
The interpretability framework (Information Flow Routes) may miss finer-grained interactions compared to more computationally intensive methods like activation patching.
future_direction: Incorporate more diverse datasets, additional model variants, and alternative interpretability techniques.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) acquire and store factual knowledge is crucial for enhancing their interpretability and reliability. In this work, we analyze the evolution of factual knowledge representation in the OLMo-7B model by tracking the roles of its attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) over the course of pre-training. We classify these components into four roles: general, entity, relation-answer, and fact-answer specific, and examine their stability and transitions. Our results show that LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses. Once the model reliably predicts answers, some components are repurposed, suggesting an adaptive learning process. Notably, attention heads display the highest turnover. We also present evidence that FFNs remain more stable throughout training. Furthermore, our probing experiments reveal that location-based relations converge to high accuracy earlier in training than name-based relations, highlighting how task complexity shapes acquisition dynamics. These insights offer a mechanistic view of knowledge formation in LLMs.

papers.title: Explainable Knowledge Graph Embedding: Inference Reconciliation for Knowledge Inferences Supporting Robot Actions
papers.research_question: How can we explain the inferences of a knowledge graph embedding to non-experts, and can such explanations help correct erratic robot behaviors due to incorrect knowledge inferences?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an inference reconciliation framework that uses a decision tree-based interpretable model to explain knowledge graph embedding inferences to non-experts, enabling them to correct erroneous robot behaviors.
papers.conclusion: The proposed inference reconciliation framework effectively explains knowledge inferences to non-experts, leading to improved interpretability and robot task performance.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed graph feature model (using decision trees and localized training) achieves statistically significant higher F1-Fidelity (98.9%) compared to the prior XKE method (87.9%).
User studies show a significant preference for knowledge-graph-based explanations when users ask knowledge inference 'why questions' and for causal-link-based explanations for causal 'why questions'.
Non-expert feedback based on the explanations leads to a 117% relative improvement in link-prediction MRR and a 33.7% relative improvement in robot task success rate.
Ablation studies confirm that using decision trees (vs. linear regression) and localized training (vs. using all relation paths) are crucial for high classification fidelity.
The framework is demonstrated in a household robot domain, where explanations help users identify and correct nonsensical beliefs in the robot's knowledge, improving task performance.
papers.abstract: Learned knowledge graph representations supporting robots contain a wealth of domain knowledge that drives robot behavior. However, there does not exist an inference reconciliation framework that expresses how a knowledge graph representation affects a robot's sequential decision making. We use a pedagogical approach to explain the inferences of a learned, black-box knowledge graph representation, a knowledge graph embedding. Our interpretable model, uses a decision tree classifier to locally approximate the predictions of the black-box model, and provides natural language explanations interpretable by non-experts. Results from our algorithmic evaluation affirm our model design choices, and the results of our user studies with non-experts support the need for the proposed inference reconciliation framework. Critically, results from our simulated robot evaluation indicate that our explanations enable non-experts to correct erratic robot behaviors due to nonsensical beliefs within the black-box.

papers.title: Linear representations in language models can change dramatically over a conversation
papers.research_question: How do linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models change over the course of a conversation?
papers.core_contribution: Linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models can change dramatically over the course of a conversation, flipping their meaning, which challenges static interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Representational dynamics over conversations pose challenges for interpretability and safety (e.g., static probes may be misleading), but also point to new research directions for understanding contextual adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of factuality and ethics can flip over a conversation (e.g., in opposite day prompt).
These changes are content-dependent: generic information is preserved, while conversation-relevant information flips.
Changes occur across different model families and layers of the model.
Changes happen even when replaying off-policy conversations (scripts from other models).
Larger models show more dramatic representational changes.
papers.limitation: Evaluated a relatively small set of conversations due to the need to tailor question sets to each conversation.
future_direction: Understanding how models' representations change in various applications (e.g., codebases).
Developing more robust interpretability and safety methods that account for representation dynamics.
Methods to control adaptability (increase or decrease) for safety.
papers.abstract: Language model representations often contain linear directions that correspond to high-level concepts. Here, we study the dynamics of these representations: how representations evolve along these dimensions within the context of (simulated) conversations. We find that linear representations can change dramatically over a conversation; for example, information that is represented as factual at the beginning of a conversation can be represented as non-factual at the end and vice versa. These changes are content-dependent; while representations of conversation-relevant information may change, generic information is generally preserved. These changes are robust even for dimensions that disentangle factuality from more superficial response patterns, and occur across different model families and layers of the model. These representation changes do not require on-policy conversations; even replaying a conversation script written by an entirely different model can produce similar changes. However, adaptation is much weaker from simply having a sci-fi story in context that is framed more explicitly as such. We also show that steering along a representational direction can have dramatically different effects at different points in a conversation. These results are consistent with the idea that representations may evolve in response to the model playing a particular role that is cued by a conversation. Our findings may pose challenges for interpretability and steering -- in particular, they imply that it may be misleading to use static interpretations of features or directions, or probes that assume a particular range of features consistently corresponds to a particular ground-truth value. However, these types of representational dynamics also point to exciting new research directions for understanding how models adapt to context.

papers.title: Hyperdimensional Probe: Decoding LLM Representations via Vector Symbolic Architectures
papers.research_question: How do LLMs represent concepts internally during analogy completion and text generation? Can VSA-based probing capture these latent features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hyperdimensional Probe, a VSA-based probing method that unifies input-oriented feature extraction and output-oriented analysis to decode LLM representations.
papers.conclusion: The Hyperdimensional Probe successfully captures latent features in LLM representations using VSA, unifying prior probing methods and providing insights into conceptual representations during inference.
papers.key_findings:
The Hyperdimensional Probe effectively extracts meaningful concepts from LLM representations across diverse models and tasks.
Models differ in conceptual richness; e.g., OLMo-2 shows richer structure than GPT-2.
Mathematical analogies tend to have sparser conceptual representations.
During text generation, LLM failures may be due to loss of question-related concepts rather than answer-related concepts.
The method unifies input and output perspectives, enabling joint analysis.
papers.limitation: Dependence on unidirectional transformation that prevents causal validation and on a set of predefined features.
papers.abstract: Despite their capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain opaque with limited understanding of their internal representations. Current interpretability methods either focus on input-oriented feature extraction, such as supervised probes and Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), or on output distribution inspection, such as logit-oriented approaches. A full understanding of LLM vector spaces, however, requires integrating both perspectives, something existing approaches struggle with due to constraints on latent feature definitions. We introduce the Hyperdimensional Probe, a hybrid supervised probe that combines symbolic representations with neural probing. Leveraging Vector Symbolic Architectures (VSAs) and hypervector algebra, it unifies prior methods: the top-down interpretability of supervised probes, SAE's sparsity-driven proxy space, and output-oriented logit investigation. This allows deeper input-focused feature extraction while supporting output-oriented investigation. Our experiments show that our method consistently extracts meaningful concepts across LLMs, embedding sizes, and setups, uncovering concept-driven patterns in analogy-oriented inference and QA-focused text generation. By supporting joint input-output analysis, this work advances semantic understanding of neural representations while unifying the complementary perspectives of prior methods.

papers.title: Discovering Hierarchical Latent Capabilities of Language Models via Causal Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How can we causally evaluate language model capabilities and discover hierarchical latent capabilities from benchmark performance data while accounting for base model heterogeneity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a causal representation learning framework (Hierarchical Component Analysis) that identifies a hierarchical linear causal structure among latent language model capabilities from benchmark performance data, revealing a causal direction from general problem-solving to instruction-following to mathematical reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Controlling for base model variation is critical for uncovering causal relationships among latent capabilities, and the discovered hierarchical capability structure provides substantial scientific insights beyond simple numerical rankings.
papers.key_findings:
Performance data exhibit heterogeneity across base models, necessitating control for base model variation in evaluations.
A subset of base models (Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B) share similar latent performance patterns.
A three-node linear causal structure (general problem-solving → instruction-following → mathematical reasoning) reliably explains observed benchmark performance variations.
The causal effect from instruction-following to mathematical reasoning is stable across domains and is stronger for Qwen models compared to Llama models.
The method can impute missing benchmark performance more accurately by accounting for base model heterogeneity compared to global matrix completion.
papers.limitation: The causal model recovery can be sensitive to the choice of base models and may be affected by finite-sample errors and violations of causal assumptions.
future_direction: Further investigation of the effect of finite-sample error and violations of causal assumptions on causal graph recovery.
papers.abstract: Faithful evaluation of language model capabilities is crucial for deriving actionable insights that can inform model development. However, rigorous causal evaluations in this domain face significant methodological challenges, including complex confounding effects and prohibitive computational costs associated with extensive retraining. To tackle these challenges, we propose a causal representation learning framework wherein observed benchmark performance is modeled as a linear transformation of a few latent capability factors. Crucially, these latent factors are identified as causally interrelated after appropriately controlling for the base model as a common confounder. Applying this approach to a comprehensive dataset encompassing over 1500 models evaluated across six benchmarks from the Open LLM Leaderboard, we identify a concise three-node linear causal structure that reliably explains the observed performance variations. Further interpretation of this causal structure provides substantial scientific insights beyond simple numerical rankings: specifically, we reveal a clear causal direction starting from general problem-solving capabilities, advancing through instruction-following proficiency, and culminating in mathematical reasoning ability. Our results underscore the essential role of carefully controlling base model variations during evaluation, a step critical to accurately uncovering the underlying causal relationships among latent model capabilities.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual transformers like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate layers representing concepts in English before mapping to the target language, indicating an English bias in their internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs have an English bias in their internal representations, which may lead to linguistic biases and has implications for equitable AI.
papers.key_findings:
In translation tasks, intermediate layers decode the English version of the correct next token before switching to the target language.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space, concept space (biased towards English), and output space.
Token energy is low in middle layers, indicating that latents are in a concept space orthogonal to token space.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: What Makes a Good Reasoning Chain? Uncovering Structural Patterns in Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: What structural patterns in long chain-of-thought reasoning drive or predict the correctness of final answers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LCoT2Tree, an automated framework for converting long chain-of-thought reasoning into hierarchical tree structures, enabling structural analysis that predicts reasoning success and reveals error patterns.
papers.conclusion: LCoT2Tree is a powerful tool for diagnosing, interpreting, and improving reasoning in LLMs, highlighting the critical role of structural analysis in understanding reasoning chains.
papers.key_findings:
Structural patterns extracted by LCoT2Tree are stronger predictors of reasoning success than length-based features across diverse tasks and models.
Error patterns such as over-branching, step redundancy, direct reasoning, and skipped thinking are identified in incorrect reasoning chains.
Reasoning behaviors vary across tasks, with different structural patterns for math, code, and science tasks.
Different models exhibit distinguishable reasoning styles on the same task, as captured by LCoT2Tree.
LCoT2Tree improves Best-of-N decoding by selecting well-structured reasoning chains, enhancing accuracy in complex tasks.
papers.limitation:
Structural analysis alone cannot capture semantic errors or recognize correct reasoning that deviates from common structural patterns.
As models improve and produce more coherent reasoning by default, the value of structural diagnostics may decrease.
LCoT2Tree is computationally expensive due to reliance on off-the-shelf large language models for tree construction.
future_direction: Integrate semantic reasoning signals with structural analysis to achieve a more holistic understanding of LLM reasoning behaviors.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in reasoning with large language models (LLMs) have popularized Long Chain-of-Thought (LCoT), a strategy that encourages deliberate and step-by-step reasoning before producing a final answer. While LCoTs have enabled expert-level performance in complex tasks, how the internal structures of their reasoning chains drive, or even predict, the correctness of final answers remains a critical yet underexplored question. In this work, we present LCoT2Tree, an automated framework that converts sequential LCoTs into hierarchical tree structures and thus enables deeper structural analysis of LLM reasoning. Using graph neural networks (GNNs), we reveal that structural patterns extracted by LCoT2Tree, including exploration, backtracking, and verification, serve as stronger predictors of final performance across a wide range of tasks and models. Leveraging an explainability technique, we further identify critical thought patterns such as over-branching that account for failures. Beyond diagnostic insights, the structural patterns by LCoT2Tree support practical applications, including improving Best-of-N decoding effectiveness. Overall, our results underscore the critical role of internal structures of reasoning chains, positioning LCoT2Tree as a powerful tool for diagnosing, interpreting, and improving reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: More than Correlation: Do Large Language Models Learn Causal Representations of Space?
papers.research_question: Does the internal spatial representation in large language models have a causal effect on their behavior in geospatial tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models learn internal spatial representations of location words, and these representations causally influence the model's performance on geospatial tasks.
papers.conclusion: Through representational similarity analysis and probing, the paper shows that both DeBERTa-v2 and GPT-Neo learned spatial representations of location words, and intervention experiments demonstrate these representations have causal effects on model output.
papers.key_findings:
The hidden states of city names in DeBERTa and GPT-Neo correlate with real-world geospatial distances, as shown by representational similarity analysis.
Linear and non-linear probes can map hidden states to latitude and longitude with low error, indicating the presence of spatial information.
A novel GeoDist loss function, which accounts for spherical geometry, improves probing performance over mean squared error.
Causal intervention experiments show that aligning hidden states with true geographic coordinates improves accuracy in a country prediction task, while misaligning degrades it.
Perturbing hidden states with spatial information affects next-word prediction for country names, demonstrating causal use of spatial representations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to location words and geospatial tasks; it is unclear how spatial representations affect other types of words and non-geospatial tasks.
future_direction: Investigate spatial representations for words without inherent geographical property
Study the effect of spatial representation perturbation on tasks that do not rely on geographical knowledge
papers.abstract: Recent work found high mutual information between the learned representations of large language models (LLMs) and the geospatial property of its input, hinting an emergent internal model of space. However, whether this internal space model has any causal effects on the LLMs' behaviors was not answered by that work, led to criticism of these findings as mere statistical correlation. Our study focused on uncovering the causality of the spatial representations in LLMs. In particular, we discovered the potential spatial representations in DeBERTa, GPT-Neo using representational similarity analysis and linear and non-linear probing. Our casual intervention experiments showed that the spatial representations influenced the model's performance on next word prediction and a downstream task that relies on geospatial information. Our experiments suggested that the LLMs learn and use an internal model of space in solving geospatial related tasks.

papers.title: Learning to perform role-filler binding with schematic knowledge
papers.research_question: Can connectionist architectures perform role-filler binding, i.e., recall arbitrary fillers corresponding to a specified role, even when these pairings violate correlations seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: Networks with external memory (Fast Weights and reduced NTM) can learn role-filler binding with previously unseen fillers and without explicitly labeled bindings, and decoding analyses provide insight into how they store and retrieve bindings.
papers.conclusion: External memory components enable neural networks to learn role-filler binding, allowing them to extract relational structure from input and generalize to novel fillers and correlation-violating bindings.
papers.key_findings:
Networks with external memory (Fast Weights and reduced NTM) successfully perform role-filler binding with previously unseen fillers, while simpler networks (RNN, LSTM) fail or only solve simple roles.
Decoding analyses show that successful networks store role-filler bindings in external memory components (fast weights matrix or NTM memory buffer), while the controller's hidden state does not retain this information.
Networks can generalize to role-filler bindings that violate correlations seen during training, and can also retain statistical regularities when given ambiguous inputs.
Networks fail to perform role-filler binding when test stories are presented in a shuffled order, indicating a need for shared structural similarity between train and test examples.
The diversity of training fillers is crucial for learning role-filler binding; networks trained on a small pool of fillers fail to generalize to novel fillers.
papers.limitation: Networks fail when given stories presented in a different order (shuffled), showing they need shared structural similarity between train and test examples.
future_direction: Explore training regimes that use shuffled stories during training to make models robust to test stories with shuffled segments.
Investigate how much a pool of train fillers needs to be expanded to allow networks to learn a representation that extends to previously unseen fillers.
Test whether networks without external memory could also perform role-filler binding, e.g., with larger LSTM models.
papers.abstract: Through specific experiences, humans learn the relationships that underlie the structure of events in the world. Schema theory suggests that we organize this information in mental frameworks called "schemata," which represent our knowledge of the structure of the world. Generalizing knowledge of structural relationships to new situations requires role-filler binding, the ability to associate specific "fillers" with abstract "roles." For instance, when we hear the sentence Alice ordered a tea from Bob, the role-filler bindings customer:Alice, drink:tea and barista:Bob allow us to understand and make inferences about the sentence. We can perform these bindings for arbitrary fillers-we understand this sentence even if we have never heard the names Alice, tea, or Bob before. In this work, we define a model as capable of performing role-filler binding if it can recall arbitrary fillers corresponding to a specified role, even when these pairings violate correlations seen during training.
