Previous work found that models can learn this ability when explicitly told what the roles and fillers are, or when given fillers seen during training. We show that networks with external memory learn to bind roles to arbitrary fillers, without explicitly labeled role-filler pairs. We further show that they can perform these bindings on role-filler pairs that violate correlations seen during training, while retaining knowledge of training correlations. We apply analyses inspired by neural decoding to interpret what the networks have learned.

papers.title: From Growing to Looping: A Unified View of Iterative Computation in LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between looping and depth-growing in LLMs, and do they share a common mechanism for improving reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper unifies looping and depth-growing in LLMs, showing they share mechanistic signatures of iterative computation and can be composed to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Depth growing and looping are complementary methods for inducing iterative computation to improve reasoning, and their unification suggests a simple reasoning recipe.
papers.key_findings:
Looped and depth-grown models exhibit similar depth-wise computational signatures, including increased reliance on late layers and periodic patterns aligned with the block size.
Depth-grown models can be looped at inference time to improve reasoning performance without being trained to loop.
Looped and depth-grown models adapt better than baselines to in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning.
Depth-grown models achieve the largest reasoning gains when using high-quality, math-heavy cooldown mixtures.
The 'grow first, loop later' strategy yields the strongest reasoning performance under matched data and inference FLOPs.
papers.limitation: Tuning the baseline training hyperparameters for depth-grown or looped models may improve performance, but this is left for future work.
future_direction: Tuning the baseline training hyperparameters for depth-grown or looped models to improve performance.
papers.abstract: Looping, reusing a block of layers across depth, and depth growing, training shallow-to-deep models by duplicating middle layers, have both been linked to stronger reasoning, but their relationship remains unclear. We provide a mechanistic unification: looped and depth-grown models exhibit convergent depth-wise signatures, including increased reliance on late layers and recurring patterns aligned with the looped or grown block. These shared signatures support the view that their gains stem from a common form of iterative computation. Building on this connection, we show that the two techniques are adaptable and composable: applying inference-time looping to the middle blocks of a depth-grown model improves accuracy on some reasoning primitives by up to $2\times$, despite the model never being trained to loop. Both approaches also adapt better than the baseline when given more in-context examples or additional supervised fine-tuning data. Additionally, depth-grown models achieve the largest reasoning gains when using higher-quality, math-heavy cooldown mixtures, which can be further boosted by adapting a middle block to loop. Overall, our results position depth growth and looping as complementary, practical methods for inducing and scaling iterative computation to improve reasoning.

papers.title: Emergence and Localisation of Semantic Role Circuits in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether and how LLMs develop causally functional representations of semantic roles, specifically focusing on the localization, emergence dynamics, and cross-scale/cross-family generalization of semantic-role circuits.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COMPASS, a causal-temporal method for discovering and tracking semantic-role circuits in LLMs, and finds that these circuits are highly localized, emerge via gradual refinement, and show partial transfer across scales and architectures.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure that exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures, suggesting that transformers encode predicate-argument binding via compact circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic-role information is encoded in compact, role-specific circuits (89–92% attribution within ≤20 nodes).
These circuits emerge via continuous refinement rather than discrete phase transitions.
There is a structure-function dissociation: circuits stabilize structurally before becoming functionally indispensable.
Cross-scale and cross-family analysis shows moderate component reuse (24–51% node overlap) but divergent wiring.
Larger models reuse similar components while rewiring connections.
papers.abstract: Despite displaying semantic competence, large language models' internal mechanisms that ground abstract semantic structure remain insufficiently characterised. We propose a method integrating role-cross minimal pairs, temporal emergence analysis, and cross-model comparison to study how LLMs implement semantic roles. Our analysis uncovers: (i) highly concentrated circuits (89-94% attribution within 28 nodes); (ii) gradual structural refinement rather than phase transitions, with larger models sometimes bypassing localised circuits; and (iii) moderate cross-scale conservation (24-59% component overlap) alongside high spectral similarity. These findings suggest that LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure, and these mechanisms exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures.

papers.title: MindCraft: How Concept Trees Take Shape In Deep Models
papers.research_question: How do neural networks internally construct and consolidate abstract concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MindCraft framework and Concept Trees to systematically trace how abstract concepts emerge, branch, and stabilize across layers in deep models.
papers.conclusion: MindCraft provides a hierarchical reconstruction of a model's reasoning process, offering a significant step towards building transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Trees reveal a hierarchical, tree-shaped organization of concept separation within models, with more salient concepts branching earlier.
The method captures conceptual importance shaped by context, not just token embedding distances.
Propagation patterns of counterfactual differences are consistent across diverse tasks, indicating a robust hierarchical dynamic.
Concept separation layers are disentangled from input embedding distances, highlighting the framework's ability to analyze high-level conceptual organization.
The framework is applicable across multiple model architectures and scales, demonstrating generality.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-modal domains.
Using the identified Concept Paths to perform precise, surgical edits on model behavior.
Exploring the compositional 'algebra' of how multiple concepts interact within the network's learned representation space.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models demonstrate strong performance across language, vision, and reasoning tasks. However, how they internally structure and stabilize concepts remains elusive. Inspired by causal inference, we introduce the MindCraft framework built upon Concept Trees. By applying spectral decomposition at each layer and linking principal directions into branching Concept Paths, Concept Trees reconstruct the hierarchical emergence of concepts, revealing exactly when they diverge from shared representations into linearly separable subspaces. Empirical evaluations across diverse scenarios across disciplines, including medical diagnosis, physics reasoning, and political decision-making, show that Concept Trees recover semantic hierarchies, disentangle latent concepts, and can be widely applied across multiple domains. The Concept Tree establishes a widely applicable and powerful framework that enables in-depth analysis of conceptual representations in deep models, marking a significant step forward in the foundation of interpretable AI.

papers.title: Latent Concept Disentanglement in Transformer-based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformers represent latent structures when performing in-context learning? Do they disentangle and compose latent concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that transformers disentangle and compose latent concepts during in-context learning, representing them in low-dimensional subspaces that reflect the geometry of the latent parameters.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of disentangling and composing latent concepts during in-context learning, with internal representations that capture the geometry of the underlying latent parameters.
papers.key_findings:
For multi-hop reasoning tasks, the model uses step-by-step composition of latent concepts via a sparse set of attention heads.
The bridge-resolving mechanism is much stronger in the larger 27B model compared to the 2B model, indicating model size benefits latent concept disentanglement.
Adding more in-context examples strengthens the causal importance of the relevant sub-circuits and increases concept representation disentanglement.
For numerical tasks with latent parameters, task vectors lie on low-dimensional smooth manifolds that reflect the geometry of the underlying parameter (e.g., radius).
Interpolating along the task vector manifold allows steering the model's computation, approximately interpolating the latent parameter.
papers.limitation:
Only English language queries are used, so mechanisms may differ across languages.
The latent concepts tested are all human-interpretable (e.g., numbers, countries), limiting generalization to more intricate relationships.
papers.abstract: When large language models (LLMs) use in-context learning (ICL) to solve a new task, they must infer latent concepts from demonstration examples. This raises the question of whether and how transformers represent latent structures as part of their computation. Our work experiments with several controlled tasks, studying this question using mechanistic interpretability. First, we show that in transitive reasoning tasks with a latent, discrete concept, the model successfully identifies the latent concept and does step-by-step concept composition. This builds upon prior work that analyzes single-step reasoning. Then, we consider tasks parameterized by a latent numerical concept. We discover low-dimensional subspaces in the model's representation space, where the geometry cleanly reflects the underlying parameterization. Overall, we show that small and large models can indeed disentangle and utilize latent concepts that they learn in-context from a handful of abbreviated demonstrations.

papers.title: Factual Probing Is [MASK]: Learning vs. Learning to Recall
papers.research_question: Can we interpret factual probing results as a lower bound on the factual information encoded in a language model, or do prompt-search methods learn from the training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OPTI PROMPT, a continuous prompt optimization method that improves factual probing accuracy, and shows that optimized prompts can exploit regularities in training data, complicating the interpretation of probing results.
papers.conclusion: OPTI PROMPT is an effective method for factual probing, but data-driven prompt optimization can exploit training data regularities, making it challenging to interpret probing results as a pure lower bound on model knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
OPTI PROMPT improves top-1 accuracy on the LAMA benchmark by 6.4% over previous methods.
Training data for factual probing contains regularities (e.g., class priors, lexical correlations) that can be exploited by prompt optimization methods.
Optimized prompts can predict facts even when probing randomly initialized models, indicating they learn from training data rather than solely eliciting stored knowledge.
Partitioning test facts into 'easy' (predictable from training data) and 'hard' subsets reveals that OPTI PROMPT improves on both, suggesting it is better at learning from data and eliciting facts from the language model.
Continuous prompt optimization is more efficient and effective than discrete token search, but requires white-box model access.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to determine whether a prediction comes from the language model's stored knowledge or from patterns learned from the training data during prompt optimization.
Gradient-based prompt optimization methods like OPTI PROMPT require white-box access to the model, limiting their use with API-based large models.
future_direction: Develop techniques for attributing predictions to specific training instances to better understand the source of factual knowledge.
Pursue more mechanistic explanations for how language models learn and represent factual information, beyond prompt-based probing.
papers.abstract: demonstrated that it is possible to retrieve world facts from a pretrained language model by expressing them as cloze-style prompts and interpret the model's prediction accuracy as a lower bound on the amount of factual information it encodes. Subsequent work has attempted to tighten the estimate by searching for better prompts, using a disjoint set of facts as training data. In this work, we make two complementary contributions to better understand these factual probing techniques. First, we propose OPTIPROMPT, a novel and efficient method which directly optimizes in continuous embedding space. We find this simple method is able to predict an additional 6.4% of facts in the LAMA benchmark. Second, we raise a more important question: Can we really interpret these probing results as a lower bound? Is it possible that these prompt-search methods learn from the training data too? We find, somewhat surprisingly, that the training data used by these methods contains certain regularities of the underlying fact distribution, and all the existing prompt methods, including ours, are able to exploit them for better fact prediction. We conduct a set of control experiments to disentangle "learning" from "learning to recall", providing a more detailed picture of what different prompts can reveal about pre-trained language models.

papers.title: Dynamics Reveals Structure: Challenging the Linear Propagation Assumption
papers.research_question: What structural constraints are imposed on a model’s representation if we demand that local linear updates respect the logical structure of relational knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that first-order parameter updates cannot guarantee systematic propagation of logical operations like composition due to geometric constraints, explaining failures in knowledge editing and reasoning.
papers.conclusion: First-order updates cannot guarantee logical coherence for composition, and dynamics reveals structural constraints that are invisible to static function approximation.
papers.key_findings:
For negation and converse, systematic linear propagation requires a tensor factorization separating entity-pair context from relation content.
Converse further requires decomposition into symmetric and antisymmetric components.
For composition, any conjunction-faithful linear feature map must be bilinear, which is incompatible with negation equivariance, leading to collapse.
Empirical evidence shows gradients of facts and their negations are positively aligned, contrary to the anti-alignment required by SLP.
Failures in knowledge editing, the reversal curse, and multi-hop reasoning may stem from these structural limitations.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical results assume the linear propagation regime, while real models exhibit nonlinear effects.
Focus on binary relations; extension to n-ary relations is left for future work.
future_direction: Extending to n-ary relations.
Incorporating nonlinear effects.
Exploring architectural biases that might approximate the required tensor factorization.
papers.abstract: Neural networks adapt through first-order parameter updates, yet it remains unclear whether such updates preserve logical coherence. We investigate the geometric limits of the Linear Propagation Assumption (LPA), the premise that local updates coherently propagate to logical consequences. To formalize this, we adopt relation algebra and study three core operations on relations: negation flips truth values, converse swaps argument order, and composition chains relations. For negation and converse, we prove that guaranteeing direction-agnostic first-order propagation necessitates a tensor factorization separating entity-pair context from relation content. However, for composition, we identify a fundamental obstruction. We show that composition reduces to conjunction, and prove that any conjunction well-defined on linear features must be bilinear. Since bilinearity is incompatible with negation, this forces the feature map to collapse. These results suggest that failures in knowledge editing, the reversal curse, and multi-hop reasoning may stem from common structural limitations inherent to the LPA.

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: LLM Knowledge is Brittle: Truthfulness Representations Rely on Superficial Resemblance
papers.research_question: Do LLMs learn robust underlying knowledge representations, or are they fragile and tied to the exact phrasings and formulations seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs' internal representations of statement truthfulness are brittle and degrade under superficial, semantically-preserving transformations, indicating that knowledge representations rely on superficial resemblance to pre-training data rather than robust, generalizable knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LLMs learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that fail to generalize to scenarios unlike those seen during training, presenting a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes and the reliability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness separability degrades as samples become more out-of-distribution (OOD) across all probing methods, datasets, and model families.
Certain topics (e.g., sociology, marketing) have more robust representations than others (e.g., history).
Benchmark performance does not imply robust representations; knowledge representations degrade even for questions the model answers correctly.
Larger models may not be more robust; the 70B Llama model showed the steepest degradation in some cases.
The type of transformation affects degradation differently; translation breaks representations while negation does not affect internal probe performance.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to decoder-only autoregressive language models.
Use of perplexity as a proxy for out-of-distribution (OOD) may not be perfect.
Only semantically-preserving transformations are considered.
future_direction: Improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.
Extending the analysis to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder models).
Exploring other types of distribution shifts beyond superficial transformations.
papers.abstract: For Large Language Models (LLMs) to be reliable, they must learn robust knowledge that can be generally applied in diverse settings -- often unlike those seen during training. Yet, extensive research has shown that LLM performance can be brittle, with models exhibiting excessive sensitivity to trivial input variations. In this work, we explore whether this brittleness is a direct result of unstable internal knowledge representations. To explore this question, we build on previous work showing that LLM representations encode statement truthfulness -- i.e., true, factual statements can be easily separated from false, inaccurate ones. Specifically, we test the robustness of learned knowledge by evaluating representation separability on samples that have undergone superficial transformations to drive them out-of-distribution (OOD), such as typos or reformulations. By applying semantically-preserving perturbations, we study how separability degrades as statements become more OOD, across four LLM families, five evaluation datasets, and three knowledge probing methods. Our results reveal that internal representations of statement truthfulness collapse as the samples' presentations become less similar to those seen during pre-training. While LLMs can often distinguish between true and false statements when they closely resemble the pre-training data, this ability is highly dependent on the statement's exact surface form. These findings offer a possible explanation for brittle benchmark performance: LLMs may learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that allow for only limited generalizability. Our work presents a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes, and more broadly, calls for further research on improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.

papers.title: Layers at Similar Depths Generate Similar Activations Across LLM Architectures
papers.research_question: How do the latent spaces used by independently-trained LLMs relate to one another, and do they have any universal properties?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer-based language models generate a progression of distinct activation geometries across layers, and this entire progression is largely shared across independently-trained models of different architectures.
papers.conclusion: Layers at corresponding depths from different LLMs tend to generate similar activation geometries, indicating a shared progression of representations across independently-trained models.
papers.key_findings:
Activations at different depths within the same model have different nearest neighbor relationships.
Activations at corresponding depths of different models have similar nearest neighbor relationships.
Affinity matrices comparing layers across models show diagonal structure, indicating that layers at similar relative depths are more similar.
The diagonal structure is statistically significant for every pair of models tested.
The similarity is present across a variety of input datasets, though the strength varies.
papers.limitation: The strength of diagonal structure varies across input datasets, being strongest on web text.
papers.abstract: How do the latent spaces used by independently-trained LLMs relate to one another? We study the nearest neighbor relationships induced by activations at different layers of 24 open-weight LLMs, and find that they 1) tend to vary from layer to layer within a model, and 2) are approximately shared between corresponding layers of different models. Claim 2 shows that these nearest neighbor relationships are not arbitrary, as they are shared across models, but Claim 1 shows that they are not "obvious" either, as there is no single set of nearest neighbor relationships that is universally shared. Together, these suggest that LLMs generate a progression of activation geometries from layer to layer, but that this entire progression is largely shared between models, stretched and squeezed to fit into different architectures.

papers.title: Mitigate Position Bias in LLMs via Scaling a Single Hidden States Channel
papers.research_question: How can position bias (lost in the middle) in long-context language models be mitigated by addressing positional information in hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that positional information in hidden states (besides position embeddings) contributes to position bias in LLMs, and proposes a method to mitigate bias by scaling a single channel of hidden states, improving performance on long-context tasks.
papers.conclusion: Scaling positional hidden states effectively mitigates position bias in LLMs, improving performance on long-context tasks without significant side effects, and the method is generalizable across different model architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights exhibit U-shaped patterns that correlate with position bias.
Positional information in hidden states, generated by the causal mask, is a significant cause of position bias.
Specific channels in hidden states (positional hidden states) show monotonic relationship with token position.
Scaling a single positional hidden state channel can significantly reduce position bias and improve retrieval accuracy.
The proposed method generalizes across different model architectures and tasks with minimal impact on original capabilities.

papers.title: Efficient Knowledge Probing of Large Language Models by Adapting Pre-trained Embeddings
papers.research_question: Can pre-trained embedding models be used as efficient proxies to estimate the factual knowledge acquired by large language models without making forward passes through the LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PEEK, a method that adapts pre-trained embedding models with a linear layer to efficiently estimate LLM knowledge without querying the LLM, achieving high accuracy and scalability.
papers.conclusion: PEEK provides a scalable and cost-effective framework for estimating LLM knowledge using proxy embeddings, enabling efficient identification of factual gaps before deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Sentence embedding models are more effective than graph embeddings for estimating LLM knowledge, achieving up to 90% accuracy.
PEEK works across different LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini) and knowledge datasets (DBP100k, YAGO310).
LoRA tuning does not significantly improve performance over simple linear tuning of the embedding models.
Embeddings can estimate knowledge from multiple probing strategies: binary generation, logits generation, activation prediction, and fact generation.
The method reveals that LLMs do not induce facts in the same way as path-based graph neural networks, indicating differences in knowledge representation.
papers.limitation:
Results may be confounded by hidden factors such as data leakage between embedding models and LLMs due to overlapping training data.
The method does not consider more difficult probing tasks like fill-in-the-blank or multiple choice QA, which may generate arbitrary facts harder to estimate.
Reliance on Wikipedia-derived knowledge limits generalization to specialized domains without domain-specific embeddings.
future_direction: Analyze why certain embeddings estimate LLM knowledge better than others to understand underlying mechanisms.
Use PEEK in retrieval-augmented generation to filter out already-known facts and improve context efficiency.
Explore dynamic adaptation of proxy embeddings as the LLM continues to learn from limited examples.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire knowledge across diverse domains such as science, history, and geography encountered during generative pre-training. However, due to their stochasticity, it is difficult to predict what LLMs have acquired. Prior work has developed different ways to probe this knowledge by investigating the hidden representations, crafting specific task prompts, curating representative samples, and estimating their uncertainty. However, these methods require making forward passes through the underlying model to probe the LLM's knowledge about a specific fact, making them computationally expensive and time-consuming. To bridge this gap, we propose $\textbf{PEEK}$ or $\textbf{P}$roxy $\textbf{E}$mbeddings to $\textbf{E}$stimate $\textbf{K}$nowledge of LLMs, by leveraging the pre-trained embedding models that effectively encode factual knowledge as text or graphs as proxies for LLMs. First, we identify a training set of facts known by LLMs through various probing strategies and then adapt embedding models to predict the LLM outputs with a linear decoder layer. Comprehensive evaluation on $3$ Wikipedia-derived datasets, $4$ LLMs, and $7$ embedding models shows that embeddings can predict LLM knowledge on a held-out set with up to 90 % accuracy. Furthermore, we find that sentence embedding models are more suitable than graph embeddings to predict LLM knowledge, shedding light on the underlying representation of the factual landscape. Thus, we believe that knowledge-adapted embeddings can be used to identify knowledge gaps in LLMs at scale and can provide deeper insights into LLMs' internal inductive bias. The code and data are made available at https://github.com/claws-lab/peek.

papers.title: Amnesic Probing: Behavioral Explanation with Amnesic Counterfactuals
papers.research_question: Does high probing performance indicate that the probed information is actually used by the model for prediction? The paper aims to assess the importance of a property for a task by removing it and measuring the behavioral change.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Amnesic Probing, a counterfactual method to assess the importance of a property for a task by removing it from the representation and measuring the behavioral change. Shows that high probing performance does not necessarily mean the property is used by the model.
papers.conclusion: Amnesic probing provides a richer view of how linguistic information is used by neural models compared to conventional probing, and calls for increased scrutiny of claims based on probing results.
papers.key_findings:
High probing performance does not correlate with task importance.
Some properties (like dependency and POS) are important for word prediction, while others (like phrase boundaries) are not.
The importance of properties differs between masked and non-masked settings.
Different labels within a property (e.g., different POS tags) have different impacts on word prediction.
The recovery of properties after removal varies across layers.
papers.limitation:
The method only removes linearly-present information, and the representation of properties might be intertwined.
The selectivity control is not perfect, and the intervention may remove more information than intended.
future_direction: Develop non-linear removal methods.
Further investigate the relative importance of different properties.
papers.abstract: A growing body of work makes use of probing to investigate the working of neural models, often considered black boxes. Recently, an ongoing debate emerged surrounding the limitations of the probing paradigm. In this work, we point out the inability to infer behavioral conclusions from probing results and offer an alternative method that focuses on how the information is being used, rather than on what information is encoded. Our method, Amnesic Probing, follows the intuition that the utility of a property for a given task can be assessed by measuring the influence of a causal intervention that removes it from the representation. Equipped with this new analysis tool, we can ask questions that were not possible before, e.g. is part-of-speech information important for word prediction? We perform a series of analyses on BERT to answer these types of questions. Our findings demonstrate that conventional probing performance is not correlated to task importance, and we call for increased scrutiny of claims that draw behavioral or causal conclusions from probing results.

papers.title: Distributional reasoning in LLMs: Parallel reasoning processes in multi-hop reasoning
papers.research_question: What strategy does an LLM use to solve multi-hop reasoning questions when not explicitly writing down a thought process (i.e., without chain-of-thought)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that during multi-hop reasoning, LLMs internally activate a distribution of potential intermediate answers in middle layers, and the final answer can be approximated via a linear transformation from this distribution, revealing parallel reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ a distributional reasoning process for multi-hop questions, characterized by parallel activation of intermediate possibilities and a linear transformation to final answers, bridging associative and propositional reasoning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The activation vector of potential final answers (A2) can be linearly approximated from the activation vector of potential intermediate answers (A1) extracted from middle layers, with R^2 > 0.5 on average.
Middle layers generate highly interpretable embeddings representing a set of potential intermediate answers, followed by a phase transition where A1 activations decrease and A2 activations increase.
High Spearman correlation exists between the order of top-activated A1 logits in middle layers and their corresponding A2 logits in the output layer.
The same distributional reasoning process occurs even when the model hallucinates answers (on fictitious subjects or out-of-distribution attributes).
The reasoning process is largely handled at the final token position after the middle layers, with minimal influence from other token positions.
papers.limitation:
The questions have a similar general structure; altering the structure could lead to different results.
Different prompt structures, question types, or subjects could lead the model to employ various solving strategies.
The analysis cannot account for semantic categories that lack clear representative tokens (e.g., years).
The statistical analyses do not show direct causality.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms for semantic categories lacking clear representative tokens.
Investigate direct causality in the observed process.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown an impressive ability to perform tasks believed to require thought processes. When the model does not document an explicit thought process, it becomes difficult to understand the processes occurring within its hidden layers and to determine if these processes can be referred to as reasoning. We introduce a novel and interpretable analysis of internal multi-hop reasoning processes in LLMs. We demonstrate that the prediction process for compositional reasoning questions can be modeled using a simple linear transformation between two semantic category spaces. We show that during inference, the middle layers of the network generate highly interpretable embeddings that represent a set of potential intermediate answers for the multi-hop question. We use statistical analyses to show that a corresponding subset of tokens is activated in the model's output, implying the existence of parallel reasoning paths. These observations hold true even when the model lacks the necessary knowledge to solve the task. Our findings can help uncover the strategies that LLMs use to solve reasoning tasks, offering insights into the types of thought processes that can emerge from artificial intelligence. Finally, we also discuss the implication of cognitive modeling of these results.

papers.title: How Do Vision-Language Models Process Conflicting Information Across Modalities?
papers.research_question: How do vision-language models process conflicting information across modalities?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that vision-language models exhibit biases towards one modality when processing conflicting inputs, and identifies specific attention heads that can be intervened to improve performance and control the modality preference.
papers.conclusion: VLMs encounter difficulties with conflicting inputs, and their behavioral accuracy correlates with the representational salience of the target modality. Attention head interventions can manipulate the representational salience and improve performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models show performance degradation when presented with inconsistent image-caption pairs, and different models have different modality biases.
Internal representations encode unimodal information for both modalities and can detect consistency, but the target modality is not always more salient.
The representational salience of the target modality (measured by V-Measure) strongly correlates with behavioral accuracy.
The authors identify modality-agnostic router heads and modality-specific promotion heads through attention head interventions.
Intervening on these heads can improve performance and change representational salience across datasets.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on 7b-parameter multimodal large language models, which are only a subset of vision-language models.
future_direction: Extend findings to inputs from modalities beyond text and vision (e.g., audio, spatial).
Explore circuit analysis to understand interactions among attention heads and other components.
papers.abstract: AI models are increasingly required to be multimodal, integrating disparate input streams into a coherent state representation on which subsequent behaviors and actions can be based. This paper seeks to understand how such models behave when input streams present conflicting information. Focusing specifically on vision-language models, we provide inconsistent inputs (e.g., an image of a dog paired with the caption "A photo of a cat") and ask the model to report the information present in one of the specific modalities (e.g., "What does the caption say / What is in the image?"). We find that models often favor one modality over the other, e.g., reporting the image regardless of what the caption says, but that different models differ in which modality they favor. We find evidence that the behaviorally preferred modality is evident in the internal representational structure of the model, and that specific attention heads can restructure the representations to favor one modality over the other. Moreover, we find modality-agnostic "router heads" which appear to promote answers about the modality requested in the instruction, and which can be manipulated or transferred in order to improve performance across datasets and modalities. Together, the work provides essential steps towards identifying and controlling if and how models detect and resolve conflicting signals within complex multimodal environments.

papers.title: Birds have four legs?! NumerSense: Probing Numerical Commonsense Knowledge of Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: Does and to what extent do pre-trained language models capture numerical commonsense knowledge, and how robust is this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing task and dataset (NumerSense) to evaluate numerical commonsense knowledge in pre-trained language models, finding that models perform poorly and are brittle to adversarial perturbations.
papers.conclusion: Powerful pre-trained models such as BERT and RoBERTa perform surprisingly poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge even after fine-tuning, and the introduced dataset provides a basis for future improvement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT and RoBERTa perform poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge without fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning with distant supervision improves performance but still far from human performance.
Models are brittle to adversarial examples (e.g., inserting adjectives).
Attention analysis shows that important words for numerical commonsense (subject/object) receive low attention weights.
Open-domain QA models also perform poorly on 'how-many' questions derived from NumerSense.
future_direction: Improving PTLMs' abilities to faithfully capture (numerical) commonsense.
Populating numerical facts in current commonsense knowledge bases.
Improving open-domain QA for 'how-many' questions.
Incorporating more structured inductive biases (e.g., dependencies and semantic roles) in pre-training.
Controlling bias in masked language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent works show that pre-trained language models (PTLMs), such as BERT, possess certain commonsense and factual knowledge. They suggest that it is promising to use PTLMs as "neural knowledge bases" via predicting masked words. Surprisingly, we find that this may not work for numerical commonsense knowledge (e.g., a bird usually has two legs). In this paper, we investigate whether and to what extent we can induce numerical commonsense knowledge from PTLMs as well as the robustness of this process. To study this, we introduce a novel probing task with a diagnostic dataset, NumerSense, containing 13.6k masked-word-prediction probes (10.5k for fine-tuning and 3.1k for testing). Our analysis reveals that: (1) BERT and its stronger variant RoBERTa perform poorly on the diagnostic dataset prior to any fine-tuning; (2) fine-tuning with distant supervision brings some improvement; (3) the best supervised model still performs poorly as compared to human performance (54.06% vs 96.3% in accuracy).

papers.title: Localizing Lying in Llama: Understanding Instructed Dishonesty on True-False Questions Through Prompting, Probing, and Patching
papers.research_question: How can instructed dishonesty (lying) in a large language model be localized and understood using mechanistic interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper localizes layers and attention heads responsible for instructed dishonesty in LLaMA-2-70b-chat, showing that causal interventions on just 46 heads can flip the model's behavior from lying to answering honestly.
papers.conclusion: The work contributes to understanding dishonesty in LLMs by localizing the behavior to specific layers and heads, enabling causal interventions that flip the model from lying to honesty, with the goal of informing methods to prevent such behavior.
papers.key_findings:
LLaMA-2-70b-chat can be instructed to lie on true/false questions, but this behavior is sensitive and requires careful prompt engineering, including the use of assistant response prefixes.
Linear probing and activation patching identify layers 19-23 as crucial for dishonest behavior, with representations between honest and liar prompts becoming anti-parallel after these layers.
Activation patching from an honest model into a lying model on layers 19-23 can significantly increase the liar's accuracy from 2% to 63%.
A subset of 46 attention heads within layers 19-23 (0.9% of all heads) is causally important for lying; patching these heads from honest to liar models flips the liar's behavior to be honest, and vice versa.
The intervention on the 46 heads generalizes robustly across different prompts and dataset splits (Cities, Inventions, Chemical Elements, Animals, Companies, Scientific Facts).
papers.limitation: The analysis is in a toy scenario where lying involves outputting a one-token incorrect response; realistic lying scenarios could involve arbitrarily misaligned optimization targets.
future_direction: Analyze more complex misalignments (e.g., swaying political beliefs, selling products) using similar methods to find where biases/misalignments exist.
Further mechanistic interpretability work to understand how the model elicits a truth-value representation and uses it with the system prompt to decide whether to respond truthfully.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate significant knowledge through their outputs, though it is often unclear whether false outputs are due to a lack of knowledge or dishonesty. In this paper, we investigate instructed dishonesty, wherein we explicitly prompt LLaMA-2-70b-chat to lie. We perform prompt engineering to find which prompts best induce lying behavior, and then use mechanistic interpretability approaches to localize where in the network this behavior occurs. Using linear probing and activation patching, we localize five layers that appear especially important for lying. We then find just 46 attention heads within these layers that enable us to causally intervene such that the lying model instead answers honestly. We show that these interventions work robustly across many prompts and dataset splits. Overall, our work contributes a greater understanding of dishonesty in LLMs so that we may hope to prevent it.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models: 'truth directions' are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context affect the truth-value probes in large language models, and are these probes coherently incorporating contextual information?
papers.core_contribution: Truth-value probes are context sensitive but also sensitive to irrelevant information, and truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference.
papers.conclusion: Truth-value directions are context sensitive and causally mediate inference, but probes are not fully coherent.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-value probes are sensitive to context, but also to irrelevant information.
The type of errors (consistency errors) depend on the layer, model, and data.
Probes trained without premises (no-prem) still show context sensitivity, indicating that prior beliefs are not represented independently.
Instruction-tuned models show different error patterns (more E4 errors) compared to pretrained-only models.
Truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference (intervention experiment).
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as uncovering a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions are (most) sensitive to the presence of related sentences, and how to best characterize this kind of sensitivity. We do so by measuring different types of consistency errors that occur after probing an LLM whose inputs consist of hypotheses preceded by (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these truth-value directions influences the position of an entailed or contradicted sentence along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that truth-value directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models:belief directions are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context impact the behavior of belief probes (directions predictive of truth) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the context sensitivity and consistency of belief probes across layers and models, shows belief directions are causal mediators in natural language inference, and introduces a more stable variant of Contrast Consistent Search (CCR).
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that belief directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
papers.key_findings:
Belief probes are generally context sensitive but are also sensitive to irrelevant contexts and can update probabilities incorrectly.
The type of errors made by probes depend on the layer, the model type, and the kind of data.
Belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
Instruction-tuning makes models more likely to represent prior assertions as true, even if they conflict with the model's own evaluation.
papers.limitation: The difficulty of separating hypothetical LLM 'beliefs' from commonly-held beliefs, as probes might identify features correlated with truth in the training data rather than an objective evaluation of truth.
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as getting at a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions can be described as being conditional on the preceding (related) sentences. Specifically, we quantify the responsiveness of the probes to the presence of (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences, and score the probes on their consistency. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these belief directions influences the position of the hypothesis along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the (type of) model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Does Representation Matter? Exploring Intermediate Layers in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What defines a 'good' representation in large language models, and how does the quality of intermediate representations compare to final layers across different architectures and settings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that intermediate layers of LLMs often provide better representations for downstream tasks than final layers, and reveals significant differences in representation quality and evolution between Transformer and State Space Model (SSM) architectures.
papers.conclusion: The research advances understanding of internal representation dynamics in LLMs, highlighting the pivotal role of intermediate layers and the distinct behaviors of Transformer and SSM architectures, providing guidance for model optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers on downstream embedding tasks from the MTEB benchmark.
Prompt entropy in intermediate layers is negatively correlated with MMLU performance for Transformers like Llama3, but not for SSMs like Mamba2.
Transformers exhibit greater representational variability and information compression in intermediate layers, while SSMs show more stable representations across layers.
Training effects on representation quality are most pronounced in intermediate layers, with prompt entropy decreasing and InfoNCE peaking as training progresses.
Extreme input conditions (token repetition, randomness, and length) distinctly affect prompt entropy, particularly in intermediate layers, and a bimodal entropy distribution is observed in Transformer intermediate layers with an unknown cause.
papers.limitation: The cause of the bimodal entropy distribution observed in intermediate layers of Transformer models remains unknown.
future_direction: Investigate the causes of bimodal entropy distributions in intermediate layers.
Explore the development of new metrics specifically tailored to LLMs for representation evaluation.
papers.abstract: Understanding what defines a good representation in large language models (LLMs) is fundamental to both theoretical understanding and practical applications. In this paper, we investigate the quality of intermediate representations in various LLM architectures, including Transformers and State Space Models (SSMs). We find that intermediate layers often yield more informative representations for downstream tasks than the final layers. To measure the representation quality, we adapt and apply a suite of metrics - such as prompt entropy, curvature, and augmentation-invariance - originally proposed in other contexts. Our empirical study reveals significant architectural differences, how representations evolve throughout training, and how factors like input randomness and prompt length affect each layer. Notably, we observe a bimodal pattern in the entropy of some intermediate layers and consider potential explanations tied to training data. Overall, our results illuminate the internal mechanics of LLMs and guide strategies for architectural optimization and training.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Investigating task-specific prompts and sparse autoencoders for activation monitoring
papers.research_question: How do prompted probing and SAE-based probing compare for activation monitoring in language models, and under what constraints (e.g., data availability, compute) are they most effective?
papers.core_contribution: Prompted probing is a data-efficient and effective method for activation monitoring, especially in low-data regimes. SAE-based probing can be effective when inference-time compute is limited, but prompted probing is recommended when inference-time compute is available.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends prompted probing when inference-time compute is available due to its data efficiency and generalization. If inference-time compute is limited, SAE-based probing is a good alternative. Straightforward activation probing is reasonable when both inference-time and train-time compute are limited.
papers.key_findings:
Prompted last token probing is the most data-efficient technique and performs well in low-data regimes.
Prompting is important: prompted last token probe outperforms naive last token probe, especially in low-data regimes.
In high-data regimes, all probing techniques (prompted probing, SAE probing, raw last token probing) can outperform zero-shot model output.
SAE max-pooled probing generalizes poorly out-of-distribution compared to prompted probing in some cases.
For sentiment classification, last token probes perform best, and max-pooling across tokens degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
The work does not compare the methods to fine-tuning the model, which is often the method of choice when labeled training data is available.
Estimates of zero-shot monitoring performance are likely pessimistic due to lack of prompt engineering and not using reasoning models or chain-of-thought.
Few-shot prompting did not improve performance in the studied settings, possibly due to context length limitations or the model's inability to extract useful signal.
future_direction: Exploring unsupervised approaches like LAT Scans for monitoring when labeled data is unavailable.
Investigating the mechanisms underlying prompted probing and whether prompted and un-prompted probing rely on shared representations.
More research into model organisms of emergent deceptive monitors to understand collusion risks.
papers.abstract: Language models can behave in unexpected and unsafe ways, and so it is valuable to monitor their outputs. Internal activations of language models encode additional information that could be useful for this. The baseline approach for activation monitoring is some variation of linear probing on a particular layer: starting from a labeled dataset, train a logistic regression classifier on that layer's activations. Recent work has proposed several approaches which may improve on naive linear probing, by leveraging additional computation. One class of techniques, which we call "prompted probing," leverages test time computation to improve monitoring by (1) prompting the model with a description of the monitoring task, and (2) applying a learned linear probe to resulting activations. Another class of techniques uses computation at train time: training sparse autoencoders offline to identify an interpretable basis for the activations, and e.g. max-pooling activations across tokens using that basis before applying a linear probe. However, one can also prompt the model with a description of the monitoring task and use its output directly. We develop and test novel refinements of these methods and compare them against each other. We find asking the model zero-shot is a reasonable baseline when inference-time compute is not limited; however, activation probing methods can substantially outperform this baseline given sufficient training data. Specifically, we recommend prompted probing when inference-time compute is available, due to its superior data efficiency and good generalization performance. Alternatively, if inference-time compute is limited, we find SAE-based probing methods outperform raw activation probing.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Editing Language Model-Based Knowledge Graph Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can language model-based knowledge graph embeddings be edited efficiently to update or add facts without retraining the entire model?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a new task of editing language model-based knowledge graph embeddings and introduces a strong baseline, KGEditor, which efficiently edits or adds facts by updating additional parametric layers via a hypernetwork.
papers.conclusion: The proposed task of editing language model-based KG embeddings and the KGEditor method enable efficient, localized updates to factual knowledge, opening new avenues for maintaining accurate and up-to-date knowledge representations.
papers.key_findings:
KGEditor outperforms existing knowledge editing baselines (KE, MEND, CALINET) on both EDIT and ADD tasks, achieving higher success rates and better knowledge locality.
Editing KG embeddings is more challenging than editing standard language models due to handling many-to-many triples.
Prompt-tuning based KG embeddings (PT-KGE) are more suitable for editing than fine-tuning based ones (FT-KGE).
The performance of editing methods degrades as the number of edited facts increases, but KGEditor and KE maintain more stable knowledge locality than MEND.
Direct fine-tuning or adapter-based tuning of the KG embedding model leads to poor knowledge locality, indicating the need for specialized editing architectures.
papers.limitation:
Handling intricate knowledge and many-to-many relations remains challenging; edited facts from such relations can bias the model towards the edited entity, overlooking other valid entities.
Experiments are conducted on relatively small KGE models based on BERT, not on large-scale generative models (LLMs).
future_direction: Design models to edit knowledge with many-to-many relations more effectively.
Integrate large language model (LLM) editing techniques for scaling to larger generative models.
papers.abstract: Recently decades have witnessed the empirical success of framing Knowledge Graph (KG) embeddings via language models. However, language model-based KG embeddings are usually deployed as static artifacts, making them difficult to modify post-deployment without re-training after deployment. To address this issue, we propose a new task of editing language model-based KG embeddings in this paper. This task is designed to facilitate rapid, data-efficient updates to KG embeddings without compromising the performance of other aspects. We build four new datasets: E-FB15k237, A-FB15k237, E-WN18RR, and A-WN18RR, and evaluate several knowledge editing baselines demonstrating the limited ability of previous models to handle the proposed challenging task. We further propose a simple yet strong baseline dubbed KGEditor, which utilizes additional parametric layers of the hypernetwork to edit/add facts. Our comprehensive experimental results reveal that KGEditor excels in updating specific facts without impacting the overall performance, even when faced with limited training resources. Code and datasets will be available at https://github.com/AnonymousForPapers/DeltaKG.

papers.title: A Relational Inductive Bias for Dimensional Abstraction in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What is the impact of a relational bottleneck on the learning of factorized representations and generalization in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The relational bottleneck inductive bias promotes learning of factorized representations, improving generalization efficiency and aligning network behavior with human cognitive biases.
papers.conclusion: The relational bottleneck induces factorized, compositional representations that approximate human coding efficiency and processing flexibility.
papers.key_findings:
Relational networks learn faster and achieve better out-of-distribution generalization than standard feedforward networks.
Relational networks develop orthogonal, factorized representations of feature dimensions in their embeddings.
Relational networks reproduce human-like regularity biases in geometric oddball detection tasks.
Relational networks show more robust representation of stimulus regularity compared to standard contrastive models like SimCLR.
The benefits of relational processing extend to various tasks including visual reasoning and analogy.
papers.abstract: The human cognitive system exhibits remarkable flexibility and generalization capabilities, partly due to its ability to form low-dimensional, compositional representations of the environment. In contrast, standard neural network architectures often struggle with abstract reasoning tasks, overfitting, and requiring extensive data for training. This paper investigates the impact of the relational bottleneck -- a mechanism that focuses processing on relations among inputs -- on the learning of factorized representations conducive to compositional coding and the attendant flexibility of processing. We demonstrate that such a bottleneck not only improves generalization and learning efficiency, but also aligns network performance with human-like behavioral biases. Networks trained with the relational bottleneck developed orthogonal representations of feature dimensions latent in the dataset, reflecting the factorized structure thought to underlie human cognitive flexibility. Moreover, the relational network mimics human biases towards regularity without pre-specified symbolic primitives, suggesting that the bottleneck fosters the emergence of abstract representations that confer flexibility akin to symbols.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: Constructing Benchmarks and Interventions for Combating Hallucinations in LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the optimal strategies for intervening in LLMs to mitigate hallucinations, and how can we construct benchmarks to evaluate such interventions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the WACK method for constructing per-LLM hallucination benchmarks and performs a comprehensive investigation of intervention strategies, including a novel dynamic intervention that intervenes only when needed.
papers.conclusion: The WACK framework provides a way to create knowledge-based hallucination datasets and offers insights into effective intervention strategies, with attention intervention and pre-answer vectors being particularly effective.
papers.key_findings:
Intervening using pre-hallucination inner states for the steering vector is better than post-hallucination.
Intervention on the residual stream compromises the model's language modeling capability, which is mitigated to some extent by dynamic intervention.
